title: Rare David Bowie self-portrait heading to auction at Sotheby's London.
summary: A 1996 self-portrait by David Bowie , unseen in public for nearly three decades, is going under the hammer at Sotheby's London for the first time. The work, estimated at £35,000–55,000 ($46,000–$72,500), is on public view ahead of Sotheby’s Modern British and Irish Art Day Auction on October 15. Bowie gifted the painting to his St. Ives gallerist, who sold it to a private collector shortly after. The portrait has remained in that collection ever since. Done on paper, the portrait shows Bowie staring directly at the viewer, with the composition emphasizing his signature anisocoria, the condition that gave him famously mismatched-looking eyes. Bowie’s handprints can be seen pressed onto the lower corners of the artwork, lending it an unusually physical trace of the artist. The painting belongs to a group of eight large-scale self-portraits Bowie made during a prolific mid-1990s painting period. This version is widely regarded as the most expressive of the set. The bold color and gestural brushwork reflect Bowie’s long-standing interest in German Expressionism , which took root during his Berlin years recording Low, Heroes, and Lodger between 1976 and 1979, as well as his admiration for School of London painters Frank Auerbach and Leon Kossoff , both of whom he collected works by. “There's something incredibly direct and personal about this self-portrait,” said Jen Hardie, Sotheby's director and senior specialist of Modern British and Irish art. “Bowie looks straight out at you, and his own handprints appear on the work itself. It’s bold, colorful and unmistakably Bowie, capturing the same restless creativity that ran through everything he did. It also feels particularly special to see a work like this return to Sotheby's, a decade after our landmark ‘Bowie/Collector’ sale celebrated the extraordinary breadth of his own collection.” That 2016 sale saw Sotheby's London offer more than 350 works from Bowie’s personal collection, totaling £32.9 million ($43.5 million) and setting 59 individual artist auction records. The self-portrait’s debut marks a rare opportunity to encounter Bowie not through the art he acquired, but through work he made himself. Bowie also had a sharp eye as a collector. A Jean-Michel Basquiat painting he bought at Christie’s in 1995 for $93,400 resold at Phillips in 2025 for $6.59 million. His legacy as a cultural icon has proven equally powerful in the auction room. The famous photograph used for his Aladdin Sane album cover, showing Bowie with his eyes downcast and a multicolor lighting bolt painted across his face, sold for £380,000 ($502,000) at Bonhams last November, a record for album artwork.

title: Rising Artist Khalif Tahir Thompson Paints the Vanishing Brooklyn of His Childhood
summary: Playground, 2026 Khalif Tahir Thompson Victoria Miro A young Black man pushes a stroller down a sidewalk. The baby's bare feet kick out from the stroller and into the open air. A black wrought-iron fence appears behind them, and behind that a brightly colored playground and a towering set of brick buildings. It’s a setting typical of New York public housing. But this seemingly quotidian scene is inflected with a sense of the fantastical. The sidewalk appears a bright, glowing orange, a tree branch deep purple. Large numbers and letters, in vibrant hues, hover over the scene’s buildings and jungle gym, imbuing the scene with a sense of childhood imagination. The painting, Playground (2026), is typical of Brooklyn artist Khalif Tahir Thompson , one of the hottest talents of the moment. Thompson has all the telltale markers of the next big thing. He earned his MFA from Yale in 2024 and was selected for Kehinde Wiley ’s Black Rock Senegal residency in 2022. His colorful, tender portraits, inspired by family photos, as well as his imagination, are held in the collections of the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture, the Rubell Museum, Pérez Art Museum Miami , and the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston. This week, the buzzy artist opened his major London solo debut at Victoria Miro , just ahead of Frieze London (the gallery announced the representation of Thompson in April). Two Brothers, 2026 Khalif Tahir Thompson Victoria Miro For an artist with so much momentum and success, it might seem surprising that the 31-year-old’s transatlantic solo debut is inspired, in part, by a 1970s ballad about loss, regret, and mistimed love. Titled “Send in the Clowns,” the exhibition, on view through November 7th, nods to Stephen Sondheim’s song of the same name, written for the 1973 musical A Little Night Music . The wry song, most famously performed by singer Sarah Vaughan, brings a theatrical humor to the singer’s tale of disappointments. “The reference reflects the layered facets of my life and experiences, the ways we deploy humor to mask vulnerability,” said Thompson during a visit to his Bushwick studio this past August, “And it speaks to how I respond to tragedy.” When we spoke, the painter was putting the final touches on the 10 paintings that make up the show. These new works come from a place of self-reflection. In the year since turning 30, he said, he’s been in a contemplative place. “I’m in a phase of looking at my upbringing, my artistic upbringing, my motivations and ambitions as an artist, and my personal story: what stories I find interesting, and the things that come together to represent me,” he said. Thompson has earned his growing reputation with his textured, patterned, and colorful portraits rooted in his own family history. While he’s painted the figure since high school, he only turned to painting personal subjects during the pandemic. Inspired by Alice Neel ’s portraits of her friends and peers, which he saw during the Metropolitan Museum of Art ’s exhibition of her work in 2021, he decided to seek out his late grandmother Betty’s family photo albums. The Rain, 2026 Khalif Tahir Thompson Victoria Miro Betty had won the lottery in 1989, and in a bit of family lore, moved from Brooklyn to Orlando, Florida. “She was a huge archivist, like a lot of grandmothers, just a bit of a hoarder. She had a collection of Jet magazines, videotapes upon videotapes, albums upon albums,” said Thompson. Those photographs served as the basis for a pivotal series of work rooted in family history and unspoken legacies. “I started thinking about history, about the Great Migration,” said Thompson, of the albums’ effect on his worldview. “If you’re in the city, you don’t think about it. I’m from Brooklyn, and I wondered how I got here. My grandparents were from North Carolina. That’s what the albums provided.” While these vintage family photographs have shaped Thompson’s practice for the past five years, in his newest works he turns to more recent family history—his own childhood. “A lot of the imagery I’ve worked with before is from before I was alive, the ’70s, ’80s, and ’90s.…I wanted to continue with that language and do something personal, but more current,” he said. In these paintings, Thompson’s three older siblings become the main protagonists. Two Brothers (2026), for instance, is based on an early-2000s family photo of his older brothers at ages 16 and 17. The brothers appear styled and serious, one donning a faux hawk and colored contacts. The image is a time capsule, not only of fashion, but of affection. “This is how I remembered them then, from the perspective of me as a child and how I saw them,” he said of the painting. Pearl (2026), meanwhile, takes inspiration from a photograph of his sister. In the painting, she is shown standing in front of a bedroom dresser and mirror, wearing an ethereal white ensemble. The painting is Thompson’s reimagining of Whistler ’s Symphony in White, No. 1: The White Girl (1862). “When the art historical comes in, I play into it,” said Thompson of the reference. “I thought there was something very Whistler about [ Pearl ]. I got out a Whistler book, and I saw that it looked almost the same, before I’d even finished mine.” Such nods crop up throughout the show, with references to Toulouse-Lautrec , Stuart Davis , and Kees van Dongen , along with stylistic allusions to Kerry James Marshall , Lynette Yiadom-Boakye , Barkley Hendricks , and, in collage-like passages, Jasper Johns . Here, Thompson also pushes beyond the richly patterned interiors he is known for and depicts the outdoor life of the city with new dynamism. Playgrounds, hair salons, and apartment buildings all appear as key subject matter. Arch Diner, 2026 Khalif Tahir Thompson Victoria Miro “Being from Canarsie, growing up in Brooklyn, I was excited to do something very New York,” he said. While the paintings are full of color and character, they also act as a love letter to a New York that is now lost. A sense of mourning tinges the works. Thompson made a conscious effort to paint places that no longer exist for this exhibition, among them, the now-closed 24-hour Arch Diner in Canarsie. “I’ve wanted to paint the diner for a while, [as well as other] intimate spaces like that, where I spent time growing up,” he said. “The painting is about the passage of time and things that are no longer there.” Thompson’s contemplation of absence goes beyond places to people, too. “There are relationships that are no longer there, too.…brothers that don’t speak…things that happen,” he said. It’s bittersweet, with a slightly melancholy undertone. “Send in the Clowns” is about missed opportunity, a kind of silver lining.”

title: Yasmin Berrada’s Surprising Journey to Running One of Morocco's Most Important Art Galleries
summary: Orange Moon, replica after the 1984 original, 1984 Mohamed Melehi Loft Art Gallery Yasmine Berrada never set out to run a gallery. Born and raised in Casablanca, Morocco, she studied at Université Paris Dauphine and built a career in asset management before stepping away when her first daughter was born. “I was unwell at the time, and I wanted to explore something new,” she recalled to Artsy. “When I look back now, I think the art found me, more than the other way around.” Art has always been part of her life. Her father was an avid collector of Moroccan painting, and Berrada spent her first paycheck on an artwork. In 2009, she opened Loft Art Gallery with her sister Myriem in Casablanca’s Triangle d’Or district. Neither had formal art training, but both had inherited their father’s passion. “We were driven above all by passion, and by the desire to create a space that reflected who we were,” she said. “Somewhere lively and accessible, where people could discover artists but also meet them, exchange with them and better understand their work.” Some 17 years later, Loft has become a prominent champion of Moroccan modernism, helping bring the country’s artists to international audiences. In 2024, it became the first Moroccan gallery to exhibit at Art Basel . This October in London, it will make its Frieze Masters debut with a solo presentation of works by Mohamed Melehi , a defining figure of the Casablanca Art School. The milestone comes just weeks after Loft opened a new space in its hometown. Building a gallery—and an audience When the sisters founded the gallery, Casablanca’s art scene was “much more intimate than it is today,” Berrada recalled. There were few institutions or galleries where audiences could encounter contemporary art, despite the city’s rich artistic history. In the 1960s, artists Farid Belkahia , Mohamed Chabâa , and Melehi had transformed the local École des Beaux-Arts into a center for a radical new Moroccan modernism. Following independence from France in 1956, they rejected European academic conventions and colonial-era Orientalist imagery, instead drawing on local visual traditions, including Amazigh carpets, jewelry, and architecture. Their work helped forge a new artistic identity for Morocco. Untitled, 2002 Farid Belkahia Loft Art Gallery Sans titre, 2003 Farid Belkahia Loft Art Gallery For Berrada, championing this history became central to Loft’s mission. The sisters built close relationships with the Casablanca Art School’s pioneers, organizing exhibitions and publishing research on their work. But establishing a gallery also meant cultivating an audience from scratch. “We couldn’t simply exhibit work and wait for people to walk through the door,” she said. “We had to create curiosity.” Many buyers were accustomed to purchasing directly from artists, often without considering how individual works might form a collection. The sisters sought to build “a real culture of collecting,” while fostering long-term relationships with artists. “It required a lot of energy,” Berrada said, “but it also gave us tremendous freedom.” Bringing Moroccan modernism to the world That commitment extended beyond Morocco. As Loft’s roster grew to include artists from across Africa and Europe, Berrada began introducing their work to international audiences. Over the years, the gallery has participated in fairs including Art Basel Qatar , Art Basel Paris , Paris Photo , The Armory Show , and Art Dubai , while maintaining a decade-long presence at 1-54 London . In 2024, its international endeavors made it one of Artsy’s breakout galleries of the year . The Moroccan market has matured considerably, Berrada said; “10 or 15 years ago, we had to explain everything.” Yet she believes there is still work to do, particularly in securing international recognition for Moroccan artists and establishing the gallery’s role in sustaining their careers. Untitled, 1967 Mohamed Melehi Loft Art Gallery That mission takes center stage at Frieze Masters, where Loft will present “Wave Forms,” a solo exhibition tracing Melehi’s signature wave motif from 1960 to 1980. Known for his vibrant, undulating abstractions, often painted in industrial cellulose paint on wood panels, Melehi developed a visual language that connected Moroccan traditions with international modernist movements. The presentation begins with Untitled (1960), made during his years in Rome, when the wave was still emerging within his abstract compositions. Minneapolis (1962), created shortly after his move to the United States, marks another stage in his development. In 1963, Melehi exhibited alongside hard-edge painters at New York’s Museum of Modern Art . Untitled, 1960 Mohamed Melehi Loft Art Gallery Loft has championed Melehi since its earliest days, when, Berrada recalled, “it wasn’t easy to sell his work or to position it in context, even in Morocco.” Today, his work belongs to collections including Tate, the Centre Pompidou , Mathaf , and the Institut du Monde Arabe. Yet Berrada believes his wider contribution remains underappreciated. “There has been a huge evolution between how Melehi was seen when we started the gallery and how he’s seen now,” she said. “But internationally, and within art history, his work still needs to be fully established.” For her, Frieze Masters offers an opportunity to place Melehi within a more expansive narrative. “His work goes far beyond the history of Moroccan art,” she said. “It belongs to a much broader history of modernism, and we want to show that.” Untitled, 2021 Saâd Hassani Loft Art Gallery Untitled, 2026, 2026 Abdelkrim Ghattas Loft Art Gallery The fair debut follows the opening of Loft’s new Casablanca space with “Hamasāt al-Fajr,” a cross-generational exhibition bringing Moroccan modernists into dialogue with younger artists. The same week as Frieze Masters, Loft will also return to 1-54 London with works by Moroccan painter Amina Rezki and Ghanaian painter James Mishio . “Exhibiting at Frieze and 1-54 at the same time is a challenge for a small team,” Berrada admitted, “but it was very important for us to keep presenting our artists at 1-54.” Staying rooted in Morocco Despite Loft’s growing international profile, Berrada remains deeply committed to Casablanca and Marrakech. Asked whether she would consider opening another gallery abroad, she was resolute. “First we need to be truly well rooted in Morocco,” she said. “I’m not going to open in a city because I have to, because it’s a trend, or because I hear it’s the place to be.” Perhaps it is that rootedness that makes the international encounters so meaningful. Berrada describes the emotion of watching collectors in New York, Abu Dhabi, or London connect with a Moroccan artist’s work without knowing the artist or their country. “A work can come from a very personal or local story and still speak to someone on the other side of the world,” she said. “At that moment, borders somehow disappear.” Her ambition is for Loft to become “more and more of an essential international gallery while remaining true to who we are.” Yet her measure of success remains personal. “I always say the greatest compliment someone in the art world can give me is to say they trust my eye.”

title: Gap and Whitney Museum collaborate on Roy Lichtenstein collection.
summary: Clothing retailer Gap has teamed up with the Whitney Museum of American Art and the Estate of Roy Lichtenstein on an 18-piece apparel collection timed to the museum's forthcoming exhibition “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New,” which opens October 11th. In the “Gap–Lichtenstein–Whitney” collection, the artist's Pop -era imagery, including Crying Girl (1963), Standing Explosion (Black) (1965), and Cathedral #2 (1969), appears across hoodies, button-downs, graphic T-shirts, a varsity jacket, and accessories like a baseball cap, scarf, and knitted throw. The retail partnership coincides with the opening of “Like New,” a survey of more than 130 works spanning six decades of Lichtenstein’s career, co-curated by Meg Onli, the Whitney's Nancy and Fred Poses curator, and artist Alex Da Corte . The exhibition examines Lichtenstein’s recurring interest in duplication, mass media, and the circulation of images, a theme the museum’s retail team said made the artist a natural fit for a mass-market collaboration. “This artist's practice is deeply connected to popular culture and the process of reproduction,” said Jack Sachs, the Whitney’s director of retail and licensing, in a statement. “We wanted to pose the question: what does Roy's work mean to consumer culture today?” Prices range from $28 for a pair of socks modeled on Lichtenstein’s Sock (1962) to $138 for a Standing Explosion varsity jacket. Three styles, including a Cathedral #2 sweatshirt, will be sold exclusively at the Whitney’s museum store. The collection launched October 7th at select Gap stores, on Gap.com, and at shop.whitney.org. Frank Avila-Goldman, executive director of arts and intellectual property at the Estate of Roy Lichtenstein, called the collection a way of “crystallizing the brilliance, joy and wit of Roy Lichtenstein into a wearable collection” through a pairing of “three American classics.” The Whitney has teamed up with retail brands before. Last fall, the museum partnered with the New York label Bode on an eight-piece capsule collection inspired by Alexander Calder 's work Calder's Circus (1926–31), tied to the centennial exhibition “High Wire: Calder's Circus at 100.” The Museum has also maintained a long-running relationship with Max Mara, which has produced its architecturally inspired Whitney Bag since the museum's 2015 move to its Renzo Piano –designed downtown building, including a 2020 edition that was inspired by Florine Stettheimer 's Sun (1931).

title: 10 Must-See Shows During Frieze London 2026
summary: 11pm, 2026 Cece Philips Public Gallery Mountain dog, 2026 Joana Galego Soho Revue October is when London’s art world turns the volume all the way up. While Frieze London and Frieze Masters take over Regent’s Park, PAD London draws the more design-inclined to Berkeley Square, and suddenly there are more exhibitions, openings, and events than anyone could hope to get around. London’s galleries know they have an audience and plan their calendars accordingly, opening some of their biggest exhibitions of the year while everyone is in town. This year, there is plenty to pull you away from the fair tents. Goodman Gallery hosts the global premiere of a new stop-motion film by William Kentridge , one of South Africa’s most celebrated living artists, while Nicola Turner sends a mass of wool and horsehair up the Georgian façade of Annely Juda Fine Art . Soho Revue welcomes Portuguese painter Joana Galego back to Greek Street. And across town in East London, NEVEN presents sculptures made from discarded shoes by Adam Lewis Jacob. There’s a lot going on. So here, Artsy highlights 10 gallery exhibitions to catch across London during Frieze week 2026. William Kentridge “ A Nicely Built City ” Goodman Gallery Through Nov.7 A Nicely Built City (Never Resists Destruction), 2026 William Kentridge Goodman Gallery William Kentridge could just be South Africa’s greatest living artist. Back in 1993, Goodman Gallery gave his debut stop-motion animation a platform in his first exhibition with the Johannesburg-based gallery. That film became the first in Drawings for Projection (1989–present), his series of stop-motion films. More than 30 years on, Kentridge is now on film number 12, with A Nicely Built City (Never Resists Destruction) (2026), premiering at Goodman’s London space. Across the series, Kentridge has traced the changing face of Johannesburg, and South Africa more broadly, from the final years of apartheid through the decades that followed. Made over nine months in Kentridge’s Johannesburg studio, the new film begins with the 2023 methane explosion beneath Bree Street, which tore open a section of the city center. Kentridge’s stop-motion process sees charcoal drawings repeatedly photographed, erased, and redrawn, leaving ghostly traces of earlier images as Johannesburg shifts before our eyes. The film is joined by new sculptures, and editioned works on paper, alongside workshop footage from Kentridge’s debut at opera house Glyndebourne earlier this year, where he directed a production of Monteverdi’s L’Orfeo . Lucy Dodd “ The good, the true and the beautiful ” Sprüth Magers Through Oct.24 Moss moon, 2026 Lucy Dodd Sprüth Magers New York–born artist Lucy Dodd makes large abstract paintings built from loose washes, stains, splashes, and pools of color, often using unconventional pigments in place of traditional paint. Her latest body of work was born out of her recent move from upstate New York to Scotland’s Moray Coast, where she began drawing the materials of her new surroundings directly into the paintings. For her exhibition at Sprüth Magers , for example, she’s used burnt peat washed down the Findhorn River after the 2025 Dava Moor wildfires. Other materials include local herbs, spirulina algae, cochineal made from crushed insects, copper ink, and powdered meteorite. Artemis, the Greek goddess of the hunt, wilderness and moon, provides a starting point for these new paintings, with Dodd connecting her to both her grandmother Diana and Diana, Princess of Wales. The goddess’s associations with the moon and the hunt carry into the works themselves: Dodd presents paintings in rounded and teardrop forms, which variously recall a lunar disc, a huntress’s target, an eye or a breast. Khalif Tahir Thompson “ Send in the Clowns ” Victoria Miro Through Nov.7 Arch Diner, 2026 Khalif Tahir Thompson Victoria Miro Brooklyn-born Khalif Tahir Thompson graduated from Yale with an MFA in painting and printmaking in 2024. Two years later, he makes his London solo debut with “ Send in the Clowns ” at Victoria Miro . Thompson’s large, densely worked paintings place figures in domestic and neighborhood scenes, layering earthy ochers, greens, and burgundies with patterned clothing and interiors, handmade paper and fabric, letters, and numbers. The new works look back to the Black American aesthetics of the early 2000s and Thompson’s own Brooklyn childhood. Many begin with photographs from albums belonging to his grandmother Betty, which spent 16 years in storage after her death. Siblings and relatives appear alongside people Thompson cannot identify, though he doesn’t attempt to recreate the photographs exactly. He borrows people, poses, and details, then builds his own scenes around them. The characters that we see form what Thompson calls an “imagined experience.” Nicola Turner “ I Tear Secrets From Your Yielding Flesh ” Annely Juda Fine Art Through Nov.7 Transitional Object, 2026 Nicola Turner Annely Juda Fine Art Echo in the Memory, 2026 Nicola Turner Annely Juda Fine Art If you’ve been around Hanover Square recently, you may have noticed something dark and hairy crawling up and around the entrance of Annely Juda Fine Art. It belongs to U.K.-based artist Nicola Turner, whose first solo exhibition with the gallery spills from ground floor, through the entrance, and onto its Georgian façade in a mass of wool and horsehair. Turner’s installations often respond to the histories of their surroundings, and here she has plenty to work with. The building once housed the Royal College of Chemistry, where William Henry Perkin discovered the first synthetic purple dye, and later the couturier Reville & Rossiter, which made royal gowns and writer Vita Sackville-West’s wedding dress. Turner picks up these histories by including dressmaking scissors, scientific instruments, and salvaged furniture, tangled among hand-sewn forms made from wool and horsehair reclaimed from old mattresses. Moving through the building like a wedding or funeral procession, the installation references secrecy, female shame, and the inherent memory of materials. William Crozier “ Dance of the Living 1961-1974 ” Flowers Oct.14–Nov.14 Untitled (Figure), 1961 William Crozier Flowers Portumna, 1962 William Crozier Flowers Glasgow-born artist William Crozier emerged in London in the late 1950s with dark, unsettling landscapes, but by the following decade the human figure had taken over. Influenced by the existentialist ideas he encountered in Paris and his memories of World War II newsreels, Crozier began painting isolated figures and skeletons in landscapes that seem to share their anxiety. This exhibition focuses on that pivotal period, bringing together paintings from the 1960s and early 1970s, including three early skeletal portraits and two large-scale drawings never previously exhibited. Crozier drew on medieval danses macabres and the prints of Mexican artist José Guadalupe Posada , while refusing to locate his landscapes in any particular place. Figures appear engulfed by streaks of vivid color, their surroundings as agitated as they are. By 1975, Crozier felt he had exhausted the subject and abandoned the figure altogether, returning to landscapes in which the viewer supplied the human presence. Edmond Brooks-Beckman “ Persistent Undoing ” Cob Oct.10–Nov.14 Estranged Passions, 2026 Edmond Brooks-Beckman Cob Edmond Brooks-Beckman ’s paintings look as though they have been through a lot. Thick passages of oil paint are scored, gouged, and partially stripped back, revealing glimpses of what was there before. Born in London in 1987, Brooks-Beckman completed his MA in painting at the Royal College of Art in 2023 and has developed a practice in which revising and reworking a painting is central to how it is made. For “ Persistent Undoing ” at Cob , on Bloomsbury’s Lamb’s Conduit Street, Brooks-Beckman uses this process to explore how family histories and cultural memories are passed down, altered, or lost over time. Earlier layers remain buried within the paintings, while fragments of letters and symbols resurface without necessarily being legible. Brooks-Beckman describes himself as interested in “manipulation after the first event,” piling marks on top of one another before scooping sections away or cutting around them. Scratches, half-covered words, and patches of earlier color remain visible across the finished paintings. Joana Galego “ Different Ways of Saying ” Soho Revue Through Oct.31 They could have thorns, 2026 Joana Galego Soho Revue Joana Galego’s first solo show at Soho Revue in 2023 caught Artsy’s attention, landing the Portuguese painter on our “ Artists on Our Radar ” that same year. Now she returns to the Greek Street gallery, known for championing emerging artists, with “D ifferent Ways of Saying .” Born in Cascais, Portugal, in 1994, Galego studied painting at the University of Lisbon before moving to London, where she studied at the Royal Drawing School in 2017. She now lives and works in South London. Galego’s paintings begin with a mixture of observation, photographs, imagination and her own experiences. Figures emerge through loose drawing, washes of color, and layered compositions, with some passages carefully described and others barely there. A child peers from behind a bunch of flowers; hands reach towards golden leaves; elsewhere, a couple cradles a newborn. These intimate scenes are typical of Galego’s recurring interests in memory, isolation, connection and the difficulties of communicating with one another. Jim Amaral “ A Study of Five Decades ” LAMB Through Nov. 28 Per-se Nº 014, 2001 Jim Amaral LAMB Kaleidoscope: Bottom-up Dream, 2015 Jim Amaral LAMB California-born artist Jim Amaral has lived in Bogotá since 1957, developing a surrealist practice spanning drawing, sculpture, collage and, for a period, painting. “ A Study of Five Decades ” at LAMB ’s Mayfair gallery brings together works on paper from the 1960s to the 2010s, tracing his fascination with the body, dreams, desire, and the subconscious. Hands sprout from ears, lips appear in palms, and human anatomy merges with plants in Amaral’s strange, precisely drawn world. Among the earliest works on show are black-and-white drawings from the 1960s, made as Amaral became immersed in Jungian psychoanalysis and began looking to dreams and the subconscious for imagery. His 1970s works “Love Letters,” meanwhile, have roots in early correspondence exchanged with artist Olga de Amaral, now his wife of nearly 70 years (wonderfully, their romance began while dancing the tango as students in Michigan). Alongside the exhibition, LAMB makes its Frieze Masters debut with a Spotlight devoted to Amaral’s “Invisible Flowers” (1979–80), a series of botanical drawings in which flowers bloom with human reproductive organs. Adam Lewis Jacob “Short Vamps for Long Wear” NEVEN Through Oct. 24 If you’re looking for an East London option during Frieze Week, head to NEVEN, a young gallery focused on emerging artists whose practices engage with contemporary culture and urban life. There, Glasgow-based artist and filmmaker Adam Lewis Jacob is showing “Short Vamps for Long Wear,” a new body of sculptures made from worn and discarded shoes. A Glasgow School of Art MFA graduate, Jacob works across sculpture, moving image, and publishing, often cutting up and repurposing found material. Most of the shoes for this show were picked up cheaply in markets and charity shops. Jacob rips, twists, and turns them inside out, bringing linings, labels, and other hidden parts to the surface. Storage and transit boxes from the Scottish-Italian restaurant beneath his Glasgow studio are repurposed as displays for the sculptures. The show fits into a wider concern in Jacob’s practice with transformation, circulation, and repair, and with how objects can be altered and put to use again. Cece Philips “ All the corners that are left ” Public Gallery Through Oct. 18 Three women, 2026 Cece Philips Public Gallery Lacquered Landscape, 2026 Cece Philips Public Gallery London-based painter Cece Philips is interested in what a home can reveal about the person who lives there. For her first exhibition with Public Gallery , she treats the house as a kind of portrait, placing women, particularly women of color, at the center of its private spaces. Across 12 paintings, interiors shift between deep shadow and pools of artificial light, following the changing light of a day and often lingering in the twilight hours. Philips graduated from the Royal College of Art in 2023, by which point she had already had solo exhibitions with Peres Projects in Berlin and Post Gallery in Zürich. She has since participated in group exhibitions at Hauser & Wirth and GRIMM. Philips has long been interested in who gets to occupy and move through different spaces, as Artsy noted of her work in 2023: “The social dynamics that shroud the very real dangers faced by women of color walking alone at night cease to exist in her fantastical narratives.”

title: Gen Z spends more than twice as much on art as other generations, Art Basel and UBS report finds.
summary: Gen Z collectors are outspending every other generation in the art market by a significant margin, according to the Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026. Surveying some 3,100 high-net-worth (HNW) collectors across 10 markets, the annual report, authored by Dr. Clare McAndrew, finds Gen Z averaging $347,460 in fine art expenditure in 2025, up 19% on the previous year and more than double the average of any older generation. Average fine art expenditure across all respondents rose to $124,265 in 2025, up 13% on 2024. The findings challenge prevailing assumptions about younger collectors as cautious market participants. Gen Z accounted for nearly half of all purchases priced over $1 million in 2025 and the first half of 2026, and had by far the largest share of collectors spending over $1 million in total on fine art in H1 2026—13% versus 3% overall. Paul Donovan, chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, attributed part of the trend to generational wealth transfer, noting that 40% of Gen Z respondents entered collecting through family influence and nearly 90% retained inherited works. “At the same time, younger collectors continue to favor traditional media such as painting and sculpture, suggesting that while collecting habits are evolving, aesthetic preferences remain more consistent across generations than is often assumed,” Donovan said in a statement. Contrary to assumptions about a generation raised on social media, Gen Z collectors were the most private of any group surveyed: 39% restricted in-person access to their collections to close family, friends, and household, almost twice the share of any other generation. Online, they favored invitation-only or restricted group sharing over public disclosure, with privacy described in the report as central to their personal and cultural identity. Across all generations, 64% of HNW collectors preferred to keep their art ownership within their household or a closed circle, and among those who lent works to museums, just 17% sought full public credit. The report also identifies a striking shift in how collectors—particularly younger generations—research and discover art. Use of AI and digital tools for collecting advice rose to 22% of respondents in 2026, up from just 4% in 2024, while 72% of all collectors now conduct moderate or significant independent research before buying, up 10 percentage points from 2025. Around two-thirds of respondents viewed AI positively for artist and artwork discoverability, provenance verification, and pricing analysis. In a new study of how collectors begin building their collections, painting emerged as the primary entry point, cited as one of the first three purchases by 43% of respondents, followed by sculpture (25%), photography (17%), and works on paper and digital art (15% each). Family influence was the single most common route into collecting overall, cited by 28% of respondents and rising to 40% among Gen Z. Collector outlook remains broadly optimistic. Some 57% of respondents expected the fine art market to grow over the remainder of 2026, rising to 60% over a 10-year horizon. Price transparency and data security were cited as the leading concerns.

title: Esphyr Slobodkina, Forgotten Star of Modern Art, Finally Gets Her Comeback
summary: Women stars of abstraction were rare in New York in the 1940s, but one of the few names to stand out among the many men who saw success was Esphyr Slobodkina . The Russian-born artist pioneered a language of dynamic abstraction in New York long before it was commonplace. Yet today, she is most widely remembered for her 1940 children's book Caps for Sale , which she wrote and illustrated. The book has sold millions of copies to date. While the wide-ranging impact of her wider artistic practice has largely been overlooked, today, Slobodkina seems to finally be making her comeback. This week, New York’s Rosenberg & Co . opens “ An Unbound Creativity ,” an exhibition of Slobodkina’s works, on view through November 14th. The exhibition marks the largest gallery show of the artist’s work in New York since she passed away in 2002. The exhibition builds on the gallery’s recent presentation of her works at Independent 20th Century in September. Slobodkina’s works are also currently on view alongside those of Louise Nevelson in the traveling museum exhibition “Architects of Being” on view at the New Britain Museum of American Art. Copper Interests (Copper Treasures), 1948 Esphyr Slobodkina Rosenberg & Co. Nocturne No. 1, 1958 Esphyr Slobodkina Rosenberg & Co. During her own time, Slobodkina received plenty of acclaim. Legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim included her in the pivotal “Exhibition by 31 Women” at Art of This Century gallery in 1943, alongside works by Frida Kahlo and Leonora Carrington . Her work had been recommended to the Guggenheim by Alfred Barr, the first director of the Museum of Modern Art . A year before that, the influential collector and artist A.E. Gallatin gave her a solo exhibition at the Museum of Living Art, the first modern art museum in America. “An Unbound Creativity” at Rosenberg & Co. is a condensed survey of Slobodkina’s life and her seven-decade artistic career, showcasing, as gallery director Kadie Ross put it, “from early academic studies, her persistent devotion to abstraction, and her exploration of multi-media works in two and three dimensions.” The earliest work in the exhibition is a 1929 sketch titled Dianna , made soon after the artist’s arrival in New York City. Born in Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 1908, Slobodkina and her family relocated to Harbin, Manchuria, around 1919 to 1921, fleeing the Russian Revolution. By 1928, she had moved to New York and enrolled at the National Academy of Design. The latest work in the show is Flying Objects Immobilized (1998), an oil, pen, and ink work of intersecting geometric forms, some resembling paper airplanes. It’s an energetic work, made just four years before her death in 2002 at the age of 93. Untitled (Oval #4), 1991 Esphyr Slobodkina Rosenberg & Co. As the dozen and a half works on view in the exhibition make clear, throughout her career, Slobodkina embraced a dazzling range of materials, including drawing and painting, collage and assemblage, textiles and clothing design. She supported herself as a seamstress during the Great Depression, following the failure of her first marriage to artist Ilya Bolotowsky . Slobodkina was also a prolific author and illustrator, publishing between 22 and 24 children’s books in her lifetime, and illustrating several books by famed children’s author Margaret Wise Brown. Slobodkina remained a lifelong proponent of “non-objective art,” non-figurative work which embraces pure colors, shapes, and lines, no matter where life brought her. She was a founding member of the American Abstract Artists Group, an artist-run organization established in 1936 to promote and support abstract and non-objective art. She later served as its president from 1963 to 1966. While her paintings can feel playful and immediate, the works were the result of a complex system of composition. Her paintings began with small sketches, traced from photographs or diagrams. She overlaid images until a composition satisfied her, then scaled it up and transferred it onto a gessoed board. “This [process] allowed the artist a degree of control over the finished work but also encouraged the free play of shapes to assert their own logic,” Ross said. Though her work is often contrasted with the spontaneous approach of the Abstract Expressionists , Ross notes that “Slobodkina’s process similarly drew from notions of impulse, discovery, and intuition.” Flying Objects Immobilized, 1998 Esphyr Slobodkina Rosenberg & Co. Nails, 1978 Esphyr Slobodkina Rosenberg & Co. Slobodkina stayed an influential force in the arts late into her life. In the 1970s, she experienced a creative renaissance, creating assemblages and paintings often with a wry edge. Ross pointed to Offshore Installation (1974), an assemblage inspired by magazine images of oil rigs that reflects Slobodkina’s fascination with machinery. Collages such as South American Love (1970) and Celebration No. 2 (1970) use her own polychrome silk fabric designs from the 1930s as their foundation. How then did such a figure fade from view? “For a long time, I think the art world—and the art market—wanted to place an artist within a defining style or movement” said Ross, “Slobodkina resisted that kind of classification.” Ross added that “her highly constructed visual language did not fit comfortably within the narrative” of Abstract Expressionism that came to dominate the memory of postwar American art. Gallery founder Marianne Rosenberg describes Slobodkina as someone who “defied any particular descriptive art label and was a free spirit focused on her work and not on the expectations of others.” The recent resurgence of interest, Ross says, ties into a wider reevaluation of women artists’ practices. “Contemporary audiences seem more receptive to artists whose careers do not resolve into a single movement, medium, or signature style,” she said. “The very multiplicity that may once have made Slobodkina difficult to categorize makes her feel remarkably current.”

title: Zaha Hadid Foundation to open refurbished London building as public arts space.
summary: In the 10th anniversary year of Zaha Hadid 's death, the Zaha Hadid Foundation is reopening its former headquarters at 10 Bowling Green Lane in London as a public cultural space for architecture, design, and related arts. A press and private view is scheduled for October 29th ahead of a public opening on November 3rd. The Victorian schoolhouse, built in the early 1870s, served as Hadid's practice for more than 30 years. The foundation’s refurbishment, led by Katherine Nolan and Alex Butterworth of London-based Studio KA, restores original features including a fireplace and doorways while preserving details Hadid herself introduced, such as Z-shaped door pulls and shard-like flooring insets. The reconfigured ground floor will house galleries, a learning space, a lecture hall, and collection displays, alongside Zaha Hadid Design, which features furniture and objects by Hadid and her studio. The building’s debut exhibition, “Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance,” curated by Catherine Howe and Libby Sellers, is the Foundation's first collection-based show, tracing how Hadid’s architectural language extended into stage and set design for dance, opera, and pop music, with projects spanning her 1989 collaboration with choreographer Rosemary Butcher to her 2014 staging of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s Così fan tutte . A second gallery will debut “The Rebar Beneath,” an 11-minute video commission by multidisciplinary artist LionHeart developed through research in Hadid's archive, while illustrator Mona Chalabi has created a timeline visualization of Hadid’s life and work for the Foundation’s foyer. That will be projected onto a textile referencing an Issey Miyake coat from Hadid’s own wardrobe, now held in the collection. The reopening will be marked by “89° of Zaha Hadid,” a two-day symposium on October 30th and 31st—the latter being Hadid's birthday—organized with the Architectural Association and the Serpentine , which built her first completed structure, a temporary pavilion, in 2000. “It was Zaha's wish for the Foundation to preserve her legacy while carrying her ideas forward,” said Rana Hadid, chair of the Foundation's trustees, in a statement, calling the archive “a profound record of her work, imagination and intellectual life.” The relaunch follows a June court ruling that ended the Foundation's royalty agreement with Hadid's former practice, now operating simply as ZHA, and comes under Foundation director Aric Chen, who since 2025 has pushed to open Hadid's archive, once described by her AA tutor Rem Koolhaas as belonging to “a planet in her own orbit,” to wider public view.

title: 10 Japanese Women Artists You Should Know
summary: In the 20th century, Japan was scarred by war and marked by anxiety and alienation. Throughout the nation’s rapid industrialization and modernization, the radical women artists of the post-war period created work that demonstrated their conviction that art could liberate them and change society. They included some of the most important artists in the world, such as Yoko Ono , Yayoi Kusama , and Ruth Asawa . Against this backdrop, Mudam Luxembourg’s landmark exhibition “Kaihō: Japanese Women Artists after 1945” brings together more than 120 works by 39 of these artists. The accompanying catalogue, published by Phaidon in English, goes even deeper to reassess the ways these artists, many of whose work has never been seen outside Japan, contributed to major art movements. Japanese women’s political agency and sexual autonomy came relatively late, compared to Western countries. They voted for the first time in 1946. Birth control pills were only legalized in Japan in 1999. Despite the setbacks, several works in “Kaihō” question the reproductive and caregiving roles traditionally assigned to women. In a video called Portrait (1998), artists Yoshiko Shimada and BuBu de la Madeleine pose as a U.S. Occupation soldier and a sex worker serving the Occupation forces, respectively, using drag as a tool to critique colonial history. Mudam’s curatorial team, led by Florence Ostende and assisted by Yurika Imaseki and Anaël Daoud, have been mindful of including lesser-known diaspora artists such as painter Tomie Ohtake , who migrated to São Paulo in 1936, forging a successful career there. Also included is the second-generation Okinawan Japanese artist from Hawaii, Toshiko Takaezu , whose ceramic “Moons” sit quietly in the corner of the final room, evoking “an elemental continuum of sky, volcanic earth, and Pacific Ocean,” according to the gallery caption. “You could see this show as a manifesto of how we should be looking for global modernism,” Ostende told Artsy. “All sense of national borders and limitations were challenged. These artists did not necessarily concede to Japan’s national identity. They really exploded the boundaries.” Here are 10 post-war Japanese women artists you need to know. Taeko Tomiyama B. 1921, Kobe, Japan. D. 2021, Tokyo. Taeko Tomiyama firmly believed that art could transform society. Having spent her childhood in Japanese-occupied Manchuria, she returned to her own country in the final years of the war. Her early lithographic works documented unemployed coal miners in the 1950s during Japan’s energy revolution. She became involved in the Japan–Korea solidarity movement in the ’70s and ’80s, supporting Korean political prisoners. The artist also made a series of lithographs in protest of the violent suppression of Gwangju’s pro-democracy movement in May 1980, some of which are displayed in the gallery. A standout work in the Mudam show is Tomiyama’s exquisitely detailed, harrowing painting, The Night of the Festival of Galungan (1986). Part of her “Memory of the Sea” series, it addresses the subject of Korean “comfort women” forced to serve the Japanese military. The dark oil painting depicts the world of the dead, a throng of skeletons on one side, garishly painted masks on the other. Lower down, women’s splayed legs are served up on a plate ceremoniously. They are all coming to haunt the terrified Japanese soldiers at the bottom of the painting. Saori Akutagawa B. 1924, Toyohashi, Japan. D. 1966, Tokyo. Saori Akutagawa originally trained as a singer, but when her husband, a composer whom she met at Tokyo College of Music, complained about her singing, she turned to “the silent art of painting.” By the 1950s, she had found the outlet she needed to express “something burning inside.” Her dye-on-cloth pieces Woman (B) and Woman (I) (both 1955) open the Mudam show, immediately pulling in viewers with their bold, vivid colors. Akutagawa once said she wanted to “rekindle the laughter of ancient deities in the modern world.” Woman A, The Hawk and Princess Kasuga (1955), appears to be an abstracted portrait of the artist herself, its angular shapes bursting with explosive energy. Akutagawa would later divorce her husband. After briefly studying in L.A., she moved to New York in the 1960s. Gaining momentum in abstraction, she exhibited alongside Kusama and Yuki Katsura , using her maiden name, Yamada. Sadly, she passed away soon after at the age of 42. Takako Saito B. 1929, Sabae, Japan. D. 2025, Düsseldorf. Grinder Chess, circa 1964 Takako Saito Doyle Untitled (Handstamped Drawing), 1985 Takako Saito OSMOS After moving to New York in the early ’60s, the self-taught artist and former teacher Takako Saito became part of the Fluxus movement, joining other Japanese women artists, such as Ono, Shigeko Kubota , and Mieko Shiomi . Fluxus suited her carefree spirit and disdain for convention. Her playful works, such as Sound Chess (1964), a large chess set with pieces only distinguishable by the sound they make, are displayed in the Mudam’s expansive foyer, alongside Ono’s Mend Piece (1966/2026) and Refugee Boat (1960/2026). In the interactive series of carved wooden heads, Spielkopf (1966–87), the viewer can drop a small bead into a sculpted head, which rolls down inside it, then pops back out unexpectedly from a different hole each time. In another gallery, Saito’s Freedom Portraitspiel No. 4 ( 1992), a sculpture made of pinecones, stones, and wooden squares, arranged whimsically in a shiny metal box, is on view. Large ears stick out on each side, while small black-and-white cubes, reminiscent of her Sound Chess , are draped along the bottom as if a piece of jewelry. Kimiyo Mishima B. 1932, Osaka. D. 2024, Osaka. Kimiyo Mishima ’s delicate trompe l’oeil sculptures take up a large part of one of the galleries. Dissatisfied with the collages she had been making using collected newspaper clippings, she began transforming them into printed or painted ceramics. These works replicated everyday objects or items of trash in the ’70s, some expanding in scale in the ’80s, as in her Coca-Cola Box (1986). “To me, the most interesting thing about ceramics was that it breaks,” Mishima said. The artist was living through Japan’s rapid economic growth and emerging information society, whose anxieties around endless news cycles find an echo today in the rise of AI. “All information instantly becomes trash as soon as it is consumed,” reads a quote next to the artwork. Mishima’s childhood was shaped by war. Seeing her hometown in Osaka destroyed after emerging from an air raid shelter one day had a lasting impact. Although her husband, Shigeji Mishima, was part of the avant-garde group Gutai , Mishima chose to work independently, forging her own path to self-expression. Atsuko Tanaka B. 1932, Osaka. D. 2005, Nara, Japan. Work (TO1018), 1970 Atsuko Tanaka Whitestone Gallery Two large-scale paintings by Atsuko Tanaka dominate the gallery dedicated to new forms of abstraction. Thick with clashing colors and drizzles of paints over abstract circles, they are delightfully barmy and reflect her interest in networks, flows, and circularity. The works brim with energy and possibility. Her Work (Bell ) (1955), which the artist would call “her invisible painting,” consists of 20 electric alarm bells connected by electrical wiring and cords. At Mudam, this has been installed across the carpeted floor in front of her colorful paintings. When the push-button switch attached to the work is activated by a visitor, a loud sound is emitted, forcing us to pay attention and really “see” her work, perhaps for the first time. Celebrated for her conceptual and performance works, including the 1956 Denkifuku (Electric Dress) in which she draped her body in hundreds of fluorescent light bulbs, Tanaka was a core member of the Gutai Association. Round of Sand (1968), a film shot on a beach of Awaji Island and displayed in a gallery dedicated to the environment, we see Tanaka drawing concentric circles into the sand. She carries on drawing despite incoming waves repeatedly erasing her work. The work is emblematic of Gutai’s concerns with the dissolution of fixed form and the body’s intervention in material. Shigeko Kubota B. 1937, Niigata, Japan. D. 2015, New York. Chess II, 1975 Shigeko Kubota Galerie Hubert Winter Shigeko Kubota was overshadowed by her more famous artist husband, Nam June Paik , but she was a pioneer of video art in her own right. In 1964, she left Japan for New York, having been disappointed by the reception of her immersive solo show in Tokyo. She joined the Fluxus group and began making video installations, incorporating mirrors and water to convey her concept of “liquid reality.” In Niagara Falls (1985–87), CRT monitors, mirrors, and other reflective surfaces are arranged in a violent cascade, against which water flows into a tank filled with shards of broken glass. The work also includes amplified sounds of waterfalls, giving the installation a dangerous feeling, and references the precarity of nature’s commodification into a tourist destination. Later in life, Kubota made work about her experience of caring for Paik, following his stroke in 1996. Bringing the ups and downs of life into art was the very essence of Fluxus. Sayako Kishimoto B. 1939, Nagoya, Japan. D. 1988, Nagoya. Instead of signing her paintings with her name, Sayako Kishimoto drew an inverted triangle to denote her fervent belief that what is at the bottom of society should be placed at the top. Her magnificent, 19-meter-long scroll, 21c. Erotica Flying Machines – A Trip to the Galaxy (1983), originally a backdrop for her own live performances, has been reproduced for this exhibition. It depicts an elaborate cosmic allegory, a world inhabited by grasshoppers and butterflies, a place of love and freedom. In the series of paintings “Erotical Girls” (1983), names of women like Pansy or Dogtooth Violet are incorporated into the titles. These women are painted in bright colors, their faces heavily made up: kitsch, unnatural, and grotesque. A nearby TV monitor shows a televised address as part of her 1983 campaign for the House of Councilors. In the video, Kishimoto asks for voter support, representing Zatsuminto (Miscellaneous People’s Party), a minority Japanese political party founded and led by LGBTQ+ and social activist Takeshi “Ken” Togo. “The suppression of gay people equals the suppression of freedom of all people,” she says. Kishimoto briefly joined the Neo-Dada Organizers as the only female member of the group in 1960, while she was still a student at Tama Art University. She moved back to her hometown of Nagoya when she was diagnosed with breast cancer at age 40. The cancer would take her life nine years later. Tāri Itō B. 1951, Tokyo. D. 2021, Tokyo. Like Kishimoto, Tāri Itō was a pioneering performance artist and social activist, her work exploring embodied resistance and questioning normative gender identity. In her performance, Self-Portrait (1996), latex rubber becomes Itō’s second skin, as she blows air through a pipe to expand different areas of her body, while asking directly to the camera, “Who are you?” She answers the question herself: “I am not married; I have no child.” Finally, she reveals that she is a lesbian. Itō is quoted in the exhibition catalogue saying that her performances, like Me Being Me (1996), gave her “great joy.” She built networks of like-minded artists and activists in Japan, Europe, East and Southeast Asia, eventually founding the Women’s Art Network (WAN, 1994–2008) back in Japan. The triple disaster of the earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear power meltdown on March 11, 2011, led Itō to make one of her final performance works, I guess it’s better that radiation doesn’t have color …Sigh (2011), in which she used LED lights and fluorescent-painted latex and onions to make visible the fear of radiation. Despite the degenerative neurological illness she developed in her later years, she still joined demonstrations and participated in group exhibitions, the last of which was in 2019. Mao Ishikawa B. 1953, Okinawa, Japan. Lives and works in Okinawa. Setting out to photograph American soldiers in her hometown Okinawa’s military bases, Mao Ishikawa was soon drawn to the women working in bars in Japan’s Koza City and Kin Town, catering to the men’s needs. She wanted to capture the Okinawan women who lived “freely and uninhibitedly,” defying social contempt. Ishikawa’s early work, Red Flowers (Akabanaa) (1975–77), some of which are displayed in the exhibition, shows these women at ease in Ishikawa’s gaze, sometimes looking straight back at the lens. In a transitional section of the gallery, where the postcard-size portraits of all 39 artists are displayed, we see Ishikawa’s black-and-white self-portrait, taken after surviving cancer in 2001–02. In this photo, scars on her body are painfully visible. Her lifelong inquiry into what it means to be an Okinawan, as distinct and separate from the imposed national identity, led to her series “Here’s What the Japanese Flag Means to Me” (1993–2011), made in collaboration with the Ainu people, Burakumin, Taiwanese, and Korean residents in Japan. In her ongoing, large-scale photographic project, The Great Ryukyu Photo Scroll (2014–present), her friends and family reenact scenes from Okinawa’s history. Nobuho Nagasawa B. 1959, Tokyo. Lives and works in New York. Utsusemi, 2018 Nobuho Nagasawa Japan Society Benefit Auction Informed by her nomadic, multicultural upbringing, Nobuho Nagasawa ’s work challenges a nationalist framing of identity. The artist is known for her participatory site-responsive installations that could be climbed over and even inhabited. Nagasawa studied art, critical theory, and music in Berlin and California, spending time in Tokoname, Japan, where she studied under the ceramist Ryoji Koie , and eventually settling in New York. The artist sees ecology as inseparable from art. Her later works adapt LED technology and fiber-optic cables. In her 2013 TED Talk, Nagasawa said, “I combine the natural world—rain, wind, waves, and bird songs with human sounds, like heartbeat and voices, and I transform them into light.” In 2023, her early earthworks Noyaki (1984) and Navel of the Earth (1985) were included in the Mori Art Museum’s 20th-anniversary exhibition, “Our Ecology: Toward a Planetary Living.” In a grainy video on view in the Mudam show, the artist is shown creating one of her earthworks with a group of Tokoname residents—laughing, shouting, and being herself.

title: 5 Standout Shows to See at Small Galleries This October
summary: Chase, 2026 Hisham Sharif Ayyam Gallery In this monthly roundup, we spotlight five stellar exhibitions at small and rising galleries. Chuma Adam and Siyabonga Fani “ Catching ” 99 Loop Gallery , Cape Town Through Oct. 24 Blackness as self-actualization: Umkhondo (A Trail/Mark), 2026 Chuma Adam 99 Loop Gallery umlambo, 2026 Siyabonga Fani 99 Loop Gallery This two-person show brings together the work of South African artists Chuma Adam and Siyabonga Fani in a meditation on materials and their connections to memory. Rising artist Chuma Adam presents monochrome paintings in acrylic on umbhaco cotton, a textile traditionally used to make Xhosa ceremonial garments in South Africa. Her painting process is intensive and physically demanding, with individual, repetitive brushstrokes coalescing into a sea of gestures. Adam was born in 2001 and is based in Johannesburg. She earned an honors degree in fine arts from the University of the Witwatersrand in 2024 and was shortlisted for the Wits Young Artist Award in 2022 and 2023. Her broader practice encompasses painting, printmaking, textiles, sculpture, and drawing, exploring themes of Blackness, identity, and visibility. 99 Loop Gallery places Adam’s works in a compelling dialogue with Siyabonga Fani ’s evocative ceramic vessels. Fani has worked with clay since the 1990s, choosing recycled terra-cotta, a material that carries its own histories. He builds his works freehand, coiling the clay intuitively to create vessels that are highly glossy and marked by organic cracks and rivulets. Fani’s father was a self-taught artist, and Fani draws on paternal inheritance in his process. Fani was born in 1981 in Gugulethu, Cape Town, and currently works in Woodstock, Cape Town. His interest in ceramics emerged while he was a student at the College of Cape Town, and he founded Siyabonga Ceramics in 2013. His works were exhibited at the Investec Cape Town Art Fair, Latitudes Art Fair, and Homo Faber in Venice in 2024, and he had his first solo show, “Ndim Lo [This Is Me],” at Art Formes in Cape Town in 2025. Matija Bobičić “ The Kingdom ” Moosey , Norwich, England Through Oct. 31 The Green Hero, 2026 Matija Bobicic Moosey The Werewolf Queen, 2026 Matija Bobicic Moosey Matija Bobičić ’s acrylic-on-canvas paintings look like what might result if Jean-Michel Basquiat tried his hand at painting Biblically accurate angels. The Slovenian artist’s chimerical figures draw from science fiction, pop culture, and Balkan folklore: Baseball-capped bobbleheads, skulls, and dinosaurs all populate the creatures’ wings. In this new exhibition, Bobičić presents figures that, according to the artist, emerge from “the archetypes of Frankenstein’s monster and the cyborg, the context of the early 1990s, and the challenges of the present moment.” In The Green Hero (2026), for example, a Ninja Turtle is made up of clown-like faces and totemic masks. Bobičić has also noted his fascination with Warhammer 40,000 , a tabletop game and fictional universe whose characters inspire his figures. The artist fuses these techno-futuristic aesthetics with symbols from Balkan folklore. The artist was born in 1987 in Maribor, Slovenia, where he lives and works. He graduated from the University of Maribor with a degree in art education in 2016. Bobičić has shown with galleries including Marvin Gardens in New York (2018, 2021), Breach Gallery in Miami (2022), Allouche Gallery in Los Angeles (2022), and Alchemy Gallery in New York (2023). He also presented a solo exhibition, “Perfect Organisms,” at the Maribor Art Gallery in Slovenia, and his work has since entered the museum’s collection. Hisham Sharif “ Allusive Veil ” Ayyam Gallery , Dubai Through Oct. 30 Behind the Window, 2026 Hisham Sharif Ayyam Gallery Red Room with a Rothko, 2026 Hisham Sharif Ayyam Gallery Hisham Sharif makes his U.A.E. solo debut with “ Allusive Veil ,” an exhibition of alluring and ambiguous paintings rooted in heritage and mythology. Sharif’s technique draws on French painters, particularly Bonnard and Vuillard , and their rhythmic, almost psychedelic interiors. Yet his style is firmly contemporary, his scenes pushed to near abstraction. In the painting Behind the Window (2026), for example, the curtained plane of a window gives way to streaking horizontal lines, creating a sense of disorientation. The show also marks Sharif’s first significant use of color, a departure from the monochrome work for which he was previously known. Born in 1993 in Bahrain, Sharif is the son of artist Abdul Rahim Sharif , who trained in Paris in the 1970s. His past exhibitions include “Frightening the Dark,” his first solo show, in 2017 at the Bahrain Arts Society, and “Sharif & Sharif” in 2022 at the Bahrain Art Centre. He won the Al Dana Award at the 50th Bahrain Annual Fine Arts Exhibition and received a Recognition Award for Outstanding Work at the 45th edition. His work is in the permanent collection of the Bahrain National Museum. Granite Calimpong “ Under the Bank, Up a Narrow Valley ” Traver Gallery , Seattle Through Oct. 31 MURKY, 2026 Granite Calimpong Traver Gallery SWEET SMELLS OF HERE, 2026 Granite Calimpong Traver Gallery Seattle-based sculptor Granite Calimpong explores his relationship with the rugged California coast where he grew up and the Pacific Northwest, where he has lived for nearly two decades, through a series of odd, biomorphic, and delightful ceramic and glass works. In these pieces, Calimpong conjures iridescent surfaces, crusty formations, and mushroom-like protrusions. Made with both glass and ceramics, the works are caught in a state of material flux between earthen depth and shiny translucence, a hint at the duality of the natural world today, where ecological crisis lives alongside the splendor and magic of adaptation. Calimpong, born in 1982, is the son of California potter Conrad Calimpong. He earned a degree in interdisciplinary computing in the arts from the University of California, San Diego, where he was introduced to glass, and later an MFA in sculpture from the University of Washington in 2019. He has held residencies at the Pittsburgh Glass Center (2013) and North Lands Creative Glass in Scotland (2016), and has had recent solo shows at Traver Gallery (2023) and JamFactory in Adelaide, Australia (2023). He is also a teacher who has led workshops at Pilchuck Glass School, Penland School of Craft, and Haystack Mountain School of Crafts. Zoe Hawk “ Lost Girls ” Visions West Contemporary , Denver Oct. 9–Nov. 21 Search Party, 2026 Zoe Hawk Visions West Contemporary Portal, 2025 Zoe Hawk Visions West Contemporary Zoe Hawk paints candy-colored visions of girlhood—campfire scenes, dances, walks in the woods—but these visions are more sinister than saccharine. In Search Party (2026), for example, a group of doll-like girls walks through the snowy woods, calling out for a lost girl as a fox stalks the trees between them. In another work, The Well (2026), moody girls in knee-high socks and Mary Janes throw rocks into a stone well. These disquieting paintings suggest dark feminine rituals. They are reminiscent of the Showtime series Yellowjackets , in which a girls’ soccer team gets stranded in the woods and begins to turn on each other. Born in 1982 in St. Louis, Hawk is now based in Columbia, Missouri. She earned a BFA in studio art from Missouri State University and an MFA in painting from the University of Iowa. She has attended residencies in Ireland, Norway, Belgium, and Qatar, and at the Women’s Studio Workshop in Rosendale, New York. Her works have been included in exhibitions such as “From Pangs to Pangolins,” curated by Trenton Doyle Hancock , at Shulamit Nazarian in Los Angeles in 2018. She had a solo show, “Dreaming as the Summers Die,” at Glass Rice in San Francisco that same year, and her work was featured in Zara’s Women in Art clothing collection in 2019.

title: Annie Leibovitz photographs OpenAI's Sam Altman in Caspar David Friedrich-inspired portrait for Vanity Fair.
summary: Annie Leibovitz has photographed OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for the cover of 2026 “New Establishment” issue of Vanity Fair, accompanying a two-part interview with the magazine. The cover portrait depicts Altman from behind, hands on hips, surveying a foggy coastline from a cliff's edge. The photograph is accompanied by a line of text reading, “Sam Altman sees the future—are we in it?” The composition appears to be a restaging of German Romantic artist Caspar David Friedrich 's iconic 1818 painting Wanderer above the Sea of Fog , now held in the collection of the Hamburger Kunsthalle. The painting is considered a definitive example of the “Rückenfigur,” an artistic device showing a figure turned away in order to invite viewers to imagine themselves in the painting. Friedrich's wanderer, shown in a green overcoat, gazing out over a misty mountain landscape, has often been interpreted as contemplation of the sublime, the fog a symbol of the unknown future. In Leibovitz's interpretation, Friedrich's vision of the Elbe Sandstone cliffs in Bohemia is replaced by Bay Area bluffs, and Altman stands in as the solitary man positioned at the edge of a cliff. While Friedrich’s figure contemplated nature’s connection to divinity, Altman, it might be inferred, contemplates the future of artificial intelligence. The reference offers an uneasy inversion, with Friedrich’s figure enthralled by nature, and Altman, the artificial and technological. Altman’s cover story leads Vanity Fair’ s revived “New Establishment” list, with the tech CEO addressing AI safety lapses, government regulation, and his rivalry with Elon Musk in an interview. This is far from the first time Leibovitz has looked to art history for inspiration, linking her subjects to famed precedents for beauty, power, or interiority. In 2002, she photographed actress Salma Hayek as Frida Kahlo for Vogue , drawing on Kahlo's own self-portraiture. For a 2013 Vogue shoot, she restaged eight famous paintings using actress Jessica Chastain as her model. The cover pictured Chastain as Frederic Leighton 's Flaming June, with reimaginings of works by Vincent van Gogh , René Magritte , Félix Vallotton , and Julia Margaret Cameron accompanying the feature story. More recently, Leibovitz's August 2025 Vogue cover story styled Anne Hathaway as John Singer Sargent 's Madame X .

title: JW Anderson to host a London pop-up show with artist Cerith Wyn Evans during Frieze Week 2026.
summary: JW Anderson flagship store in Pimlico, London. The exhibition centers on a new series of 30 wind chimes that Cerith Wyn Evans developed specifically for the brand, shown alongside selected works by the artist courtesy of White Cube , his representing gallery. The show, which also brings together designers, makers, and long-standing collaborators from Anderson's creative world, is open to the public from October 15th through 20th, coinciding with Frieze London. Other works on view include ceramics by Akiko Hirai , paintings by Mary Stephenson , and sculptures by Shawanda Corbett . “A Composition” is presented in partnership with American Express, and Amex Platinum Cardmembers will receive a dedicated preview day on October 14th, ahead of the public opening. They will also receive a complimentary gift from JW Anderson and an exclusive limited-edition work on paper and bookmark with purchase. The exhibition extends Anderson's long-running involvement in the art world as both collector and curator. His personal collection includes ceramic works by artists Lucie Rie , Jennifer Lee , and Sara Flynn , as well as powerhouses of the 1980s including Peter Hujar and David Wojnarowicz . He has curated exhibitions for the Hepworth Wakefield, the Holburne Museum, and London's Thomas Dane Gallery, and in 2023 organized the group show “ On Foot ” at Offer Waterman , also in London. Anderson has also made art collaboration central to his design work. For his Dior Cruise 2027 collection, shown at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art , he worked with Ed Ruscha on a series of Dior Homme button-down shirts referencing the artist's signature lettering and shadowing. For his brand, JW Anderson, he has previously partnered with the Tom of Finland Foundation and the estate of David Wojnarowicz . “A Composition” follows other recent exhibitions at the JW Anderson store, which has developed into something of a gallery space in its own right for the brand.

title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani doubles individual artist grants in New York City to $10,000.
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su, and New York City Department of Cultural Affairs (DCLA) Commissioner Diya Vij have announced that the city will increase its grants for individual artists and small nonprofits from $5,000 to $10,000, the first such increase in nearly 20 years. Grants, which are distributed through partners in each borough, are open to artists, collectives, and small nonprofits working across film, dance, writing, painting, and other disciplines. Applications are now open in Brooklyn, the Bronx, Manhattan, and Queens. Staten Island's cycle opens in November. Alongside the increase, DCLA's Materials for the Arts program will also launch a monthly “shopping day” for grantees to access free art supplies. “Artists are working New Yorkers with the same costs as everyone else. But while rent, grocery bills, and child care costs have skyrocketed in New York City, the funding artists rely on has stayed flat,” Mamdani said in a statement. “Doubling these grants is a critical step towards making sure that the painters, musicians, filmmakers, and other artists who bring life to this city can afford to call it home.” Vij, who said she spent the past six months in town halls with working artists across the five boroughs, called the increase “our first step to deeper, more meaningful support.” Mamdani also relayed the news in a more informal Instagram announcement . In the clip, he is filmed painting at an easel across from Vij, saying, “Artists are forced to make hard choices when it comes to living in this city and getting paid. There's never been a better time to apply.” According to Hyperallergic , the news follows a $323.8 million allocation for DCLA in the city's Fiscal Year 2027 budget. It marks the highest-ever yearly appropriation for the agency, which ensures public funding to supports cultural organizations throughout New York City. A January report from the Center for an Urban Future noted that the city's resident artist population has fallen 4.4 percent since 2019, its first measurable decline in decades. The increase extends a pattern of arts investment under Mamdani , who in July announced a Groundswell Community Mural Project commissioning 12 artist-led, community-painted murals across the five boroughs for the FIFA World Cup 2026 . Mamdani has separately partnered with the Met Opera and the Theatre Development Fund to expand free and low-cost access to performances for New York residents and students.

title: Hirshhorn Sculpture Garden to reopen in October 2026 following Hiroshi Sugimoto redesign.
summary: The Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden 's Sculpture Garden in Washington, DC, will reopen on October 31st following a reimagining of the landscape by Japanese artist and architect Hiroshi Sugimoto . The project marks the most significant rethinking of the garden since American modernist architect Gordon Bunshaft conceived the Hirshhorn's distinctive cylindrical museum and sunken sculpture garden more than half a century ago. The garden first opened to the public in 1974. In 1981, landscape architect Lester Collins added additional lawns, trees, ramps, and shaded outdoor spaces. Sugimoto's intervention preserves the essential character of Bunshaft's modernist campus while creating a more open, varied, and flexible setting for the museum's collection of modern and contemporary sculpture. Central to the design is a series of monumental, stacked stone walls that divide the landscape into a sequence of distinct but interconnected spaces, including the East and Central Gardens and West Lawn. The stone offers an elemental counterpoint to Bunshaft's concrete architecture and a restrained backdrop for sculpture spanning more than a century. The redesigned garden will allow the Hirshhorn to display 50 percent more artworks outdoors. Some 24 major sculptures from Joseph H. Hirshhorn's Foundational Gift will return to view, including works by Auguste Rodin , Henri Matisse , Henry Moore , Alberto Giacometti , and Barbara Hepworth , presented in dialogue with living artists and new commissions rather than organized as a chronological survey. A wider “front door” will create at-grade sightlines into the garden from the National Mall, while five points of entry, new east and west overlooks, twice as many accessible entrances, and expanded shade and seating will make the previously secluded space more porous. An underground passageway will reconnect the garden directly to the museum, establishing a physical route between the indoor galleries, Sugimoto's landscape, and the Mall. According to the Washington Post , the overhaul also includes a revamped reflecting pool. and A rotating exhibition program will also launch with a spotlight on large aluminum figures by Yoshitomo Nara . Sugimoto's design extends his longstanding relationship with the Hirshhorn, which was the first museum to present a major retrospective of his work and, in 2018, invited him to reimagine its lobby.

title: Lee Krasner Steps Out From Pollock’s Shadow
summary: In 1957, Lee Krasner moved her painting tools and set up her studio in the barn on the property of her home in Springs, New York, a hamlet in eastern Long Island. The barn—a single-light-filled space measuring roughly 20 by 20 feet—had previously been the studio of her late husband, Jackson Pollock . But from 1957 until Krasner’s death in 1984, the barn was her domain, and there she took full advantage of the space and freedom finally afforded her, producing the most brilliant works of her career. A dazzling new exhibition, “ Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous ” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art , brings together the works of husband and wife, tracing the trajectory of their careers. The show begins with Krasner, opening with a series of abstract collage paintings from the mid-1950s made from cut-up fragments of her old canvases and drawings. It concludes with Krasner, too, closing with Past Continuous (1976), a monumental collage Krasner made from her own Cubist -inspired drawings from the 1930s from which the show takes its name. Pollock’s breathtaking drip paintings appear in the middle like a storm, a force of nature that tore through Krasner’s life. In his lifetime, Pollock had become synonymous with the barn. There, he had flung, dripped, and poured paint onto canvases unrolled across its floors. In 1949, Life magazine immortalized Pollock and his studio with a profile entitled “Is He the Greatest Living Painter in the United States?” The editorial featured photographer Martha Holmes’s now-iconic images of Pollock at work, dripping paint from a brush with a cigarette dangling from his lips. Pollock and Krasner had moved to Springs from New York City in 1945, using a loan from gallerist and collector Peggy Guggenheim for the down payment on a two-story home. They had come to the bucolic seaside town seeking an escape from the distractions and demands of city life so they could focus on their work. Pollock first worked in an upstairs bedroom and Krasner in the cramped kitchen. Later, Pollock moved his studio into the property’s barn, and Krasner took the upstairs bedroom he had vacated. In August 1956, Pollock crashed his car on the side of the road after a night of heavy drinking, killing himself and his passenger, Edith Metzger, a friend of his mistress, Ruth Kligman. Kligman, who was also in the car, survived. Krasner, who had been traveling in Europe at the time of the crash, returned immediately to plan his funeral. Slowly, in the months that followed, she returned to her practice, eventually moving her tools into the barn, close to a year after his death. For many years, the barn had smelled of the kerosene used to heat a stove, but Pollock had winterized it in 1953, insulating the walls and covering the floor with Masonite squares left over from a printing job by his brother, Sanford.
