When Krasner entered the studio in 1957, she walked on tiles that hid Pollock’s paint splatters covering the wood floor beneath. Often, stories of Krasner’s life seem to end with Pollock’s death, but in reality, she was just embarking on the most fruitful years of her artistic career. Krasner, a rising star She was born Lena Krassner in Brooklyn in 1908, the fourth of six children in a working-class, Orthodox Jewish household where English, Russian, and Yiddish mingled. Krasner rebelled early and leaned into art. She studied at the Woman’s Art School of Cooper Union, the National Academy of Design (which suspended her for entering a basement off-limits to women), and City College, before she enrolled in 1937 at the Hans Hofmann School of Fine Arts. There, as The Met’s exhibition catalogue notes, she “imbibed the tenets of Cubism and came to revere Henri Matisse .” In late 1941, the painter John Graham invited her to show in “American and French Paintings” at McMillen Inc. Krasner, who had cultivated friendships with many in the New York art world, knew every name on the list except Pollock’s. She found his address and called on him at his Eighth Street studio. “I was overwhelmed, bowled over, that’s all,” she later said. “I felt as if the floor was sinking when I saw those paintings.” By 1942, they were dating. “Krasner held the more prominent artistic reputation of the two. She was better educated and more firmly entrenched in the close-knit and pugnacious New York art world,” write curators David Breslin and Brinda Kumar in the introduction to the exhibition catalogue. Her paintings of the period “articulated still-life forms and figures in thick paint, fusing geometric shapes with organic forms in overlapping planes over flat backgrounds of white or gray,” with primary blues, reds, and yellows “knit together by strong black lines.” Mondrian was an influence, and she often recalled with pride that he admired these works. Krasner moved into Pollock’s East Eighth Street apartment in fall 1942, and they married in October 1945. A month later, with a $2,000 loan from Peggy Guggenheim, the couple bought a farmhouse and five acres in Springs, complete with a barn. An era of doubt and rebirth The move came in the middle of what Krasner called her “black-out period,” in which, as the catalogue puts it, she built up paint on her canvases but no image emerged, producing her “gray slabs.” Pollock, long in the thrall of Picasso, had finally broken with Cubism, but Krasner wasn’t ready. She said this rupture “took me two years to digest. Between 1943 and 1944 I tried to undo my Cubist orientation and produced very little work in a rather anxious situation.” But her work also took a backseat to Pollock’s career, which she championed using her connections and good graces to earn the truculent Pollock opportunities, introducing him to Robert Motherwell , Roberto Matta , and Surrealist ideas, including automatic drawing. “At the expense of her own work,” art historian Kirk Varnedoe wrote, “Krasner poured her energy and intelligence into furthering Pollock’s efforts.” Scholar Robert Hobbs reads the gray slabs of this era as Krasner grappling with news of the Holocaust, slowly emerging from Europe. Eventually, Krasner broke through this era of artistic doubt. Working in the upstairs bedroom Pollock had vacated, she made the “Little Images,” compact, impastoed canvases of “small dabs of paint intentionally placed in even adjacency” that became “a chromatic prism through which Krasner unlocked an endless palette.” In 1953, following a disappointing solo show in 1951, she began recycling her unsold canvases into large collages. Some of these works include scraps of Pollock’s discarded drawings and canvases, among them Bald Eagle (1955). In the fall of 1955, at the age of 46, Krasner opened a solo exhibition of her collage paintings at dealer Eleanor Ward’s Stable Gallery in New York, marking her second solo show in New York. While dealer Betty Parsons was the show’s only buyer, the exhibition earned strong reviews with Stuart Preston of the New York Times calling her “a good noisy colorist” and Fairfield Porter writing, in ARTnews , that her art “seems to be about nature” and makes viewers “aware of a subtle disorder greater than [they] might otherwise have thought possible.” The show marked a new era of creativity for Krasner. Pollock, in a downward spiral fueled by alcoholism, meanwhile created only one painting that year. Krasner’s crescendo After moving into the barn in 1957, Krasner’s scale and her palette changed. In early 1958, she exhibited 17 of her “Earth Green” paintings, large-scale bright abstractions seemingly inspired by nature, at Martha Jackson Gallery. Stuart Preston wrote in a review in the Times that “the sheer energy that Miss Krasner manages to generate on her picture surfaces.” Her work went well beyond her canvases, however. Krasner worked tirelessly to secure Pollock’s legacy, and became a key source for critics and curators writing about him. She collaborated on the 1958 traveling retrospective of his work and placed his estate with Marlborough Gallery. When Marlborough’s director offered to represent her too, she declined, preferring to be asked on her own terms, not as his executor. After her mother died in 1959, insomnia drove Krasner to paint at night under artificial light. The result was the “Umber” series, which the critic Cindy Nemser described as “slashing, splintered strokes of raw umber and white.” By the mid-1960s, bright colors had returned in works like Combat (year), which measures more than 5 by 13 feet, in riotous twists and folds of pink and orange color. In 1965, Krasner took a step out of Pollock’s shadow when she opened “Lee Krasner: Paintings, Drawings, and Collages,” a retrospective of her work at the Whitechapel Gallery , her first solo exhibition outside the U.S. In 1974, the curator Bryan Robertson found a box of her 1930s drawings from Hofmann’s classes. She cut them into strips and shards, and rebuilt them as canvases named for verb tenses. “I am never free of the past,” she said. “I believe in continuity… the past is part of the present which becomes part of the future.” At the end of her life, Krasner was looking to the future through her own past. The ailing artist donated her assets, made up mainly from her work and Pollock’s, to create a foundation that would support the work of young artists. The Pollock-Krasner Foundation has granted over $90 million to artists since it was established in 1985, and is the first successful foundation established by an artist, for artists.

title: Anina Major’s Giant Woven Ceramic Towers Rethink Bahamian Craft Traditions
summary: Water Tower, 2024 Anina Major TERN Gallery In Anina Major ’s sculpture Water Tower (2024), strips of woven stoneware climb upward into a 45-inch-tall column, its ombré glaze deepening from pale aqua to rich turquoise. Melted sea glass glints across its irregular surface, while sand gathers around its base. The piece exemplifies the artist’s engagement with palm plaiting, a Bahamian weaving tradition that women have passed down for generations, often as a crucial source of their own income. Major expands the woven form, giving a familiar craft language a monumental presence. In 2024, Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM) acquired the sculpture, which will appear in “ The Sacred Mangrove ,” Major’s first solo presentation at a major international institution. The show, organized by curator Jennifer Inacio, will open at PAMM on October 1st. At the museum, Major’s towering ceramic forms rise like sentinels throughout the waterfront gallery. Folkloric bottle trees create a protective presence. Shells and reused ceramic shards scatter across the ground, while a soundscape recorded on a Bahamian beach brings the acoustics of the artist’s home country into the installation. “I was thinking about the similarities between Miami and The Bahamas,” Major told Artsy. “Not just how Miami has functioned within the historical context of Bahamian culture, but this idea of connecting entities, drawing a line between the two.” With her installation, the artist intends to “command more space and prominence,” enhancing the impact she can make as she works at a larger scale. The PAMM exhibition arrives weeks after the opening of “ SOON COME HOME ,” Major’s second solo presentation with TERN Gallery in Nassau, The Bahamas, on view through October 26th. The shows honor an artist who’s nearly a decade into her unique, hybrid practice of translating plaiting into ceramics. Major began experimenting with this process while studying ceramics at the Rhode Island School of Design, where she earned her MFA in 2017. She learned plaiting through her grandmother, Saphora Alvina Timothy Newbold, known as Mar, who passed the tradition on to other women in The Bahamas. Major has since studied how weaving patterns traveled across the islands and changed from place to place, something she describes as “repetition with adaptation.” Major cuts rolled slabs of clay into thin strips, then weaves them while they are still pliable. In “The Sacred Mangrove,” she primarily uses plain weave (a simple over-under pattern that creates a checkerboard appearance), while sculptures including Rooted Sky (2026) and Forgotten Maiden No. 3 (2025) incorporate twill and reed-based patterns. Major often works early in the morning, when ideas come faster than she can realize them. She describes her process as responsive: “There’s something about the clay that tells you when it’s ready to be done,” she said. House in the Sky, 2026 Anina Major TERN Gallery Skyscraper, 2026 Anina Major TERN Gallery That extends to glazing. She said she favors a “rich, juicy” surface, with built-up layers. The kiln introduces its own variables, warping the clay or shifting a glaze in ways she cannot fully anticipate. The artist builds further richness through firing techniques and materials beyond clay. In House in the Sky (2026), on view in “SOON COME HOME,” sand and flocking meet a glossy glaze that shifts from mossy green to cream. The Kumbla (2026) pairs salt-fired stoneware with sea glass and sand, its deep blue and violet giving way to areas of pale stoneware. At first, ceramics offered Major a way to preserve the knowledge she had inherited. Her early works drew from woven bags and dolls associated with Bahamian tourism. Major remembers looking at a souvenir small enough to fit in her palm and wondering what would happen if she deconstructed and magnified it. That impulse eventually produced works like Sandcastle (2025), a roughly 1,100-pound stoneware sculpture that grew out of experiments she began during a 2023 residency at the European Ceramic Work Centre. The Kumbla, 2026 Anina Major TERN Gallery In 2025, Major settled in upstate New York, where she began renovating a former service station into a studio with room for her increasingly ambitious work. That year, Sandcastle was named a finalist for the Loewe Foundation Craft Prize . For Major, enlarging these forms is about how the traditions behind them are valued. “I’m not trying to replace souvenirs in the marketplace,” she said. “I’m actually trying to shift perception and value around that work.” As her sculptures grew, Major also began thinking about how her individual pieces could inhabit space together. Seeing Betye Saar ’s show “Serious Moonlight” at ICA Miami in 2021 brought Major to tears. “I felt seen,” she said. “I was moved by how she allows her symbolic vocabulary to expand spatially.” The exhibition showed her how individual sculptures could become part of an immersive, room-sized installation. Major also looked to Japanese American ceramic artist Toshiko Takaezu , whose Homage to Devastation Forest (1982 – 1987), exhibited in the Noguchi Museum ’s 2024 retrospective “Toshiko Takaezu: Worlds Within,” brings ceramic forms together as a sculptural landscape. In “The Sacred Mangrove,” Major pushes her work in this direction, treating the exhibition space as an environment rather than a backdrop for individual sculptures. The mangrove became her framework, connecting Miami and The Bahamas through an ecosystem native to each place. Major describes it as “connective tissue” between them. PAMM’s glass-walled space overlooking Biscayne Bay further shaped the installation, which remains visible from outside after dark. In Nassau, Major’s work is expanding through material. “SOON COME HOME” marks the first time her signature ceramic doll series (including Brassy , 2025), inspired by the straw dolls sold in Bahamian tourist markets, appears in glass. For Major, home remains a source of inspiration and a place to return to as her practice continues to evolve. “There’s this weird thing that feels like this is just the beginning,” she said.

title: Why Mary Cassatt’s Iconic Painting of a Little Girl Is So Radical
summary: “I love to paint children,” Mary Cassatt once said. “They are so natural and truthful. They have no arrière-pensée (ulterior motive).” The American-born Impressionist became one of the most influential artists of 19th-century France with her refreshingly tender portraits of mothers and children painted in loose, tactile brushstrokes. Among her most famous paintings is Little Girl in a Blue Armchair (1878), now in the collection of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C. The painting shows a young, tired-looking girl slouching in a large floral blue armchair, a small Brussels griffon dog resting in a matching chair nearby. She wears a bored expression, her limbs sprawled over the chair in exhaustion or exasperation. This frank expression captures Cassatt’s modern, secular approach to portraying children. This year marks the centennial of Cassatt’s death in 1926 at age 82. In response, many museums are honoring her life and work. The Musée d’Orsay is opening “Mary Cassatt: Being Independent” (“ Mary Cassatt: L’Indépendante” ) on October 6th, an exhibition of nearly 80 paintings, pastels, and prints. The exhibition will travel to Boston in 2027. Meanwhile, the Art Institute of Chicago is currently hosting “Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism,” which looks at her career in the years after the final Impressionist exhibition of 1886. To mark the centennial of her life, we’ve taken a closer look at Cassatt’s celebrated Little Girl in a Blue Armchair . Cassatt collaborated with Degas to create this iconic work La Petite Danseuse de 14 Ans, 1881 Edgar Degas Théo Landel Cassatt was born in 1844 in Allegheny City, Pennsylvania, to a wealthy American family. Initially, her parents resisted her ambition to become a professional artist, but by 1860, a teenage Cassatt had enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. She moved to Europe in her twenties, eventually settling in Paris, where she would live for the rest of her life. Cassatt’s early works took inspiration from the Old Masters , whom she studied closely on painting trips through Italy, Spain, and the Netherlands. Over the years, however, her brushwork loosened and her palette brightened, and she began experimenting with the asymmetrical compositions and unconventional croppings influenced by the nascent Impressionist art movement and the dawn of photography. By 1877, Cassatt’s works had come into open conflict with the French art establishment and the official Salon rejected both of her submissions that year. That rejection spurred Edgar Degas to invite her to exhibit with the Impressionists, an invitation she accepted. Degas’s friendship with Cassatt shaped Little Girl in a Blue Armchair . The girl in the painting was the daughter of friends of Degas’s, but his contribution extended far beyond that. “It was the portrait of a friend of M. Degas,” Cassatt wrote to the Parisian dealer Ambroise Vollard in 1903. “I had done the child in the armchair and he found it good and advised me on the background and he even worked on it.” Recent cleaning and infrared imaging at the National Gallery of Art have since confirmed his work on the canvas. Scholars believe Degas most likely reworked the oddly shaped patch of floor between the chairs and the play of light through the windows, and his influence has been traced through the painting’s asymmetrical composition, its bold pattern, and its tight, cropped framing—a debt to the Japanese prints he introduced Cassatt to. The little girl enacts a rebellion against adult society The psychology of the painting, however, is quintessentially Cassatt’s. The girl becomes an agent of disorder and rebellion in the tidy adult world she inhabits. Her body sprawls diagonally across the blue-and-white floral chair, cutting against the orderly lines of the upholstery. Her expression sits somewhere between boredom and open irritation, her gaze drifting sideways toward the little dog curled up in the matching armchair beside her. Her look might be one of envy. The dog, unlike her, is unencumbered by expectations. The girl is painted, not in a nursery where she might be at ease, but a fashionable drawing room, the domain of adult women. The girl fidgets under the constraints. Feminist writer Germaine Greer called the painting Cassatt’s “first real stunner,” which she saw “as an icon of the awfulness of being at once controlled by adults and ignored by them.” The composition reinforces this sense of claustrophobia, with chairs pressing in from every side. The girl’s averted gaze here becomes an assertion of her own independence—an autonomy Cassatt celebrates. The painting caused a controversy when it debuted Afternoon Tea Party, 1991 Mary Cassatt Canopy Gallery In the Omnibus, 1991 Mary Cassatt Canopy Gallery Cassatt took an interest in the lives of women and children well beyond the canvas. She was a feminist from an early age and spent her career depicting the “New Woman” of the 19th century. These women went out in society, receiving guests, going to the theater, and conquering the modern world on their own terms. Cassatt was one of these women as well. “I am independent!” she once declared. “I can live alone and I love to work.” Cassatt, unlike many of her era, did not reserve that sense of self-possession for adults. Art historian Griselda Pollock has called Little Girl in a Blue Armchair one of the most “radical” images of childhood because of its lack of sentimentality. But Cassatt’s frank depiction of childhood also put off viewers acclimated to more idealized imagery. She submitted the painting to the American pavilion at the 1878 Paris World’s Fair, and its jury rejected it. The decision infuriated Cassatt, particularly because Degas had worked on it. “I sent it to the American section of the big exposition, they refused it,” she wrote to Vollard. “I was furious, all the more so since he had worked on it. At that time this appeared new and the jury consisted of three people of which one was a pharmacist!” Cassatt never knew what had turned the jury off of the work, but in the nearly 150 years since its creation, Little Girl in a Blue Armchair has earned a much warmer reception. The painting entered the collection of the National Gallery of Art in 1983, and has remained one of the most popular works at the museum since.

title: KAWS collaborates with Absolut Vodka on limited-edition bottle and painting.
summary: KAWS has collaborated with Absolut Vodka on a new Artist Edition bottle. The design is inspired by a painting KAWS created for the project, with Absolut’s apothecary-style bottle featuring his signature “XX” motif and his signature Chum character on the front of the bottle and an image of the original painting on the back. “I am excited to join the lineage of great artists that have worked with Absolut Vodka over the decades,” KAWS said in a statement. “My goal is to allow art to meet people in unexpected places, and I hope my bottles will be enjoyed at gatherings around the world.” KAWS, whose real name is Brian Donnelly, is known for his cartoon-like figures and artworks that sit at the intersection of street culture, fine art, and commercial goods. His works have been shown at institutions including the Brooklyn Museum , the Serpentine Gallery , and the Albertina Modern in Vienna. The Absolut partnership follows a string of brand collaborations for the artist, including a 2025 appointment as UNIQLO's first artist in residence and, this past June, a redesign of the packaging for Austria's Sacher-Torte to benefit a children’s charity. The collaboration extends Absolut’s decades-long history of working with artists on its bottle. Andy Warhol painted “Absolut Warhol” in 1985, becoming the brand’s first artist-designed advertisement and prompting Warhol to recommend Keith Haring as a successor collaborator. Since the 1980s, more than 550 artists have contributed over 850 artworks inspired by the bottle, a collection now housed at Stockholm’s Spritmuseum. “Our collaboration with KAWS reimagines the iconic Absolut bottle as a witty, unexpected work of art that feels at home on a collector’s shelf or at the center of a gathering with friends,” said Caroline Begley, Absolut’s U.S. vice president of marketing, in a statement. “By bringing KAWS’ remarkable vision to one of our most iconic assets, we’re creating a cultural statement piece that celebrates creativity, self-expression and the power of art to connect people.” The Absolut KAWS Artist Edition bottle is available for pre-order at Absolut.com and will roll out to select U.S. retailers for a limited time while supplies last.

title: Chiharu Shiota’s Monumental Thread Installations Hold a Lifetime of Memories
summary: How many memories can the length of thread hold? In Chiharu Shiota ’s hands, the answer seems boundless. For the Japanese artist, thread can evoke feelings of fear and uncertainty, as well as resilience and strength. Shiota’s immersive installations in black, white, or red thread are like intricate webs that visitors can walk through, and they often include found objects like shoes, dresses, or suitcases. “When I’m weaving, it’s like meditation,” Shiota told Artsy. “For hours, I follow the same pattern, and all my feelings go into this process. If I’m anxious or my feelings are more mixed up, then you can see it in the thread.” Born in Japan in 1972 and based in Berlin, Shiota has been making thread installations for decades. Her work has earned her international renown, including major exhibitions worldwide and, in 2015, the artist represented Japan at the Venice Biennale. In “Chiharu Shiota: The Soul Trembles,” the artist’s survey at the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts (MMFA), which opened September 26th, Shiota’s evolution from painter to performer to thread-based installation artist is on full view. Today, it’s a moment of self-reflection during an illustrious career that has seen her overcoming dire health challenges. Chiharu Shiota’s early career When she began studying art in the early 1990s, however, Shiota had other disciplines in mind. “I always wanted to be a painter,” she explained, “but while studying I couldn’t paint anymore, the paint had no feeling, I had no identity with paint.” Shiota soon began exploring other media and, in 1994, she staged Becoming Painting , a performance at the Australian National University School of Art in Canberra. At the time, she had a dream that she had become a painting. For the performance, she covered herself with canvas and red enamel paint. She saw this as an “act of liberation,” she recalled. “This was the first artwork that was not a refined, polished art piece, but rather an active bodily expression that I had thrown my entire self into.” In 1996, Shiota moved to Berlin and began studying under Marina Abramović , which was actually a mix-up. Shiota thought she was going to work with fiber artist Magdalena Abakanowicz . However, as Shiota explored performance further, she became interested in creating art without the body. It was this concern that drew her to incorporate objects to stand for human presence, like suitcases, dresses, and shoes often associated with her work today. “I only work with objects that have been used and therefore have memory inside, for example I have collected old suitcases because I can see a person in each suitcase,” she said. “There is a feeling of someone present even though no one is there.” By the late 1990s, Shiota began to shift her focus to using thread as a medium. “When I started using thread, it was like I was drawing in the air,” she said. “I could put all my energy into it.” Confronting her mortality through thread The Montreal exhibition is the first North American presentation of “The Soul Trembles,” which has traveled extensively worldwide since premiering at Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum in 2019. The MMFA is the 10th venue to host the show. Spanning more than three decades of Shiota’s career, the exhibition unfolds chronologically and includes monumental installations alongside sculpture, drawings, videos, photographs of her performances, and material related to her work in theater. Planning for the exhibition began around the same time Shiota received her second cancer diagnosis in 2017. While thinking about her body, she struggled to understand where her soul fit within the tumultuous process of healing. These concerns permeate her work. In Out of My Body (2019), red leather cut to resemble a net is suspended in the air, hanging like torn skin. On the floor beneath sit bronze casts of the artist’s limbs. The piece responds directly to Shiota’s emotional state as she grappled with cancer. “She’s had moments when she’s had to face her mortality,” said Iris Amizlev, MMFA curator of special projects. “The work resembles Shiota’s body torn apart, as if she was on an assembly line. The diagnosis and healing became like a mechanical process, and she suffered terribly.” Though the survey show has been traveling for years, Shiota rebuilds the thread installations in each institution. “Every time I work with the new space, I must imagine how the artwork will change, could it become wider, smaller, or higher,” she said. “I have to visit the exhibition space before I can decide how to create it anew. Everything depends on the space.” The installations are built from countless small gestures. At the MMFA, the process took roughly three weeks with dozens of people working, including those from Shiota’s studio and students from Montreal’s Concordia University. As the installation takes shape, threads cross, knot, and stretch across the gallery. “Black thread is like a pencil line, an accumulation of black lines creates something more abstract like the night sky or the universe, red represents blood and connection, white is used for funerals in Japan; it presents an end but also a new beginning,” the artist said. Themes of connection in Shiota’s work In the installation In Silence (2002/2026), black thread fills the room, casting a dark shadow across the dimly lit space. A seemingly charred piano and chairs sit within the dense thread matrix. The work is based on a childhood memory from when Shiota was nine. At the time, her neighbor’s house caught fire and a scorched piano was left outside. While it no longer functioned, the artist recalled, she felt its beauty radiate even more than before the fire. In Uncertain Journey (2016/2026), a dense matrix of red thread flows through the large gallery. “Visitors walk through and under the installation, activating the work with their presence,” Amizlev said. Connected to the thread are several large metal boats, an object Shiota uses often to represent immigration, displacement, and the broader journey of life. “While boats can be used as guides, we all face an uncertain future together and as individuals,” Amizlev added. “These existential moments unite us across borders and cultures—it’s one of the reasons why Shiota’s work is so universally relevant.” As “The Soul Trembles” travels, the show offers Shiota a prolonged look back at her career and the themes that seem to persist. “[My practice] has always been about memory and the existence in the absence,” she said. “An empty room can still have presence. Someone wa s living there before; I can feel them even though I have never met them.” While addressing these themes, as well as myriad conditions of life that unite us as humans, Shiota leaves her work open to personal connections and interpretations. “Everyone thinks and feels differently,” she said. “Art touches people’s hearts. It’s important that we can share these feelings, inspire each other, and relate to one another.”

title: MacArthur “Genius Grant” 2026 winners include Christine Sun Kim and Rodney McMillian.
summary: The John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation has announced the recipients of its 2026 MacArthur Fellowship. Among the 20 recipients of the annual “genius grant” are visual artists Christine Sun Kim , based in Berlin, Rodney McMillian , of Los Angeles, Vincent Valdez , who splits time between Houston and San Antonio, and Chip Thomas, of Flagstaff, Arizona. Each awardee receives an $800,000 no-strings stipend, dispersed over five years. “For 45 years, MacArthur Fellows have defied boundaries by questioning conventions, crossing disciplines, and driving collective progress,” said Kristen Mack, the foundation’s vice president for communications, MacArthur Fellows, and partnerships, in a statement. “The 2026 Fellows continue that creative tradition—they explore the depths of our humanity; they reveal untold origins to modern challenges; they expand the edges of scientific inquiry and life-saving research. They show us new ways to understand the world.” Kim’s work draws attention to ableism as it relates to Deafness. She was recently the subject of a survey at the Whitney Museum of American Art and is known for series like “Degrees of Deaf Rage” (2018–19), drawings recounting moments when hearing privilege collides with Deaf life. She memorably performed the national anthem in American Sign Language at the 2020 Super Bowl. “I am an artist illuminating cultural dimensions of sound and hearing,” she said in her MacArthur announcement video. Kim, who has two children, told the New York Times the funding would let her “scale back on taking opportunities” and “be a little bit more of a mom with more flexibility in her life.” McMillian works across painting, sculpture, video, performance, and installation to examine how history, socioeconomic conditions, and public policy shape quality of life, particularly for Black Americans in the U.S. South. His works range from the 88-foot abstract painting In This Land (2019) to From Asterisks in Dockery (2012), inspired by a chapel once on Mississippi's Dockery Plantation. Valde works primarily as a painter, examining racism and the Latinx experience in the U.S. Major works include the expressionist Kill the Pachuco Bastard! (2001) to the hyperrealist, 30-foot The Beginning Is Near, An American Trilogy, Ch. 1: The City (2016), depicting hooded Klan members. Valdez’s work was the subject of a traveling survey “Just a Dream…” in 2024–25. Thomas worked as a physician on the Navajo Nation for 36 years. The artist makes large-scale public photo murals often installed in abandoned buildings across the reservation, and founded the Painted Desert Project, bringing graffiti artists to make new work there. The rest of this year's class spans economics, physics, chemistry, choreography, and literature, and includes poet Layli Long Soldier, a citizen of the Oglala Lakota Nation whose 2017 poem “He Sápa” lent its title to Jeffrey Gibson 's 2024 U.S. Pavilion presentation at the Venice Biennale.

title: 8 Contemporary Artists Inspired By René Magritte
summary: The work of René Magritte needs little introduction. Since his death in 1967, he has become one of the defining painters of the 20th century, his work influencing generations of artists while also permeating the world of popular culture at almost every level. Referenced by everyone from The Beatles to The Simpsons, his visual vocabulary—bowler-hatted men, veiled faces, enormous apples, and levitating rocks—has left a profound mark on the worlds of advertising, graphic design, film, and photography. No other artist fused the ordinary with the uncanny so seamlessly, or shifted so effortlessly between a sense of ambiguity, dread, and deadpan humor tinged with occasional vulgarity. His enigmatic paintings, such as The Treachery of Images (1929) or The Human Condition (1933), transform everyday objects, places, and figures into surreal , psychologically charged puzzles. Combining an almost hyperrealist style with jarring shifts of scale, trompe l’oeil illusions, and visual fragmentation, his works raise fundamental questions about the boundaries between reality and representation. Now, a major new exhibition at Gagosian in London seeks to trace his enduring legacy on the art world. “This is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte” (through December 12) brings together dozens of the artist’s key paintings and works on paper, setting them in dialogue with work by almost 50 contemporary artists. As Jasper Sharp, the show’s co-curator, explained to Artsy, Magritte’s influence is by no means a recent phenomenon. “You have artists who were already making work in the ’50s thinking about Magritte, so his influence was already taking shape while he was still alive.” But the idea for the current show evolved when it became clear how great a shadow his work still casts in the 21st century. “Over the past few years, I've found myself having so many conversations about Magritte, unprompted by myself, with painters, filmmakers, and photographers.” For Sharp, the explanation for this is twofold. “I think the reason that his works have such an enduring appeal is that they disclose themselves very quickly. But, like all really interesting art, they also work on a different level. They’re not completely understandable.” At the same time, his work is technically masterful, another source of inspiration for artists. As Sharp pointed ut, “ Max Ernst famously described Magritte as a collagist in paint. Which is why he’s been so influential in the graphic design industry, the music industry, and the fashion industry. The way his works are constructed with different surfaces, different depths, gives so much potential to people who want to take his ideas and run with them.” With this in mind, here are eight contemporary artists who share some affinity with Magritte’s themes and approach. The first four are featured in the Gagosian show, while the others are our own recommendations. Lenz Geerk B. 1988, Basel. Lives and works in Düsseldorf. Man holding the night sky, 2024 Lenz Geerk Roberts Projects With their muted palettes and enigmatic subject matter, the paintings of Lenz Geerk exude a strong sense of Magrittean disquiet. Like the Belgian master, his work is steeped in art history, and the figures, objects, and places he depicts seem deeply rooted in the world of dreams. In Tie III (2024), a man in a suit stands stiffly against a bare wall, gazing at his tie unfurled on the floor at his feet, while in Man Holding the Night Sky (2024), a figure stands atop a rock, unfurling a black sheet emblazoned with stars. Cryptic and mysterious, Geerk’s work carefully balances what to reveal and what to withhold. Dominique Fung B. 1987, Ottawa, Canada. Lives and works in Brooklyn, New York. Look Steadily and Intently, 2021 Dominique Fung Woaw Born in Canada, but with ancestry in Shanghai and Hong Kong, Dominique Fung ’s work is inspired by Asian artefacts encountered in museums during her youth. Reimagined through a contemporary lens, she liberates these objects from their colonial or imperialist histories, imbuing them with a new and complex life of their own. Blending older traditions of European painting—whether Baroque , Rococo , or Renaissance —with a Surrealist streak recalling Magritte and Dorothea Tanning , works such as Stray Hair (2020) and Look Steadily and Intently (2021) have a dreamlike quality that hints at unsettling narratives just beyond our grasp. And, much like Magritte, her works operate on multiple levels. Combining elements of humor and the uncanny, their sensuous and exquisitely painted surfaces conceal more serious undertones lurking beneath. Joseph Yaeger B. 1986, Helena, Montana. Lives and works in London. Joseph Yaeger’s paintings, like Magritte’s, are full of secrets. Opaque, voyeuristic, and enigmatically titled, they are charged with a noirish atmosphere of mystery and uncertainty, occupying an uneasy space somewhere between dreams and cinema stills (on which many of them are based). The faces of his figures are often veiled or obscured—by smoke, shadows, bandages, or another person’s hand—resisting any straightforward emotional or psychological interpretation. In particular, they recall iconic works by Magritte, such as The Lovers (1928) or The Son of Man (1946). Working in watercolor on gesso, his works combine technical mastery with subtle hints of decay, their scarred and cracked surfaces dusted with studio debris, evoking a pervasive sense of dread or unease that underpins so many aspects of modern existence. New works by Yaeger will go on view at Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo later this fall. Isabelle Albuquerque B. 1981, Los Angeles. Lives and works in Los Angeles. Call Me, 2024 Isabelle Albuquerque Newchild Gallery Just as Magritte would sometimes depict the human form in fragmented, transfigured, or impossible states (as in Le Viol (1934/1945), in which a naked female torso merges with a woman’s face), Isabelle Albuquerque deconstructs the physical form to create formally complex sculptures with strong echoes of the surreal. Exploring women’s experience of desire, sexuality, and violence, she combines traditional techniques with contemporary technologies like 3D scans and lifecasts of her own body to create headless, truncated, or otherwise transmuted figures. Often merging biological forms with manufactured, mundane, or mythological elements, her sculptures serve as prime examples of the ‘surreal object’, inviting any number of readings and interpretations. In the Gagosian show, her work Summertime Sadness (2024), in which a shock of fire-red human hair sprouts from a bronze cast of a dismembered arm, has definite affinities with Magritte. As Sharp pointed out, it was “the first object she suggested when we approached her for the exhibition.” Kate Meissner B. 1995, Sacramento. Lives and works in Los Angeles. Kate Meissner ’s highly saturated, theatrically lit oil paintings present a mysterious shadow world in which familiar scenes are made alluringly strange. The female figures she depicts are elusive, possessed of an eerie, plastic quality somewhere between human and mannequin. Their faces are always obscured, their bodies contorted and partially veiled by fabric, and their limbs either prosthetic or missing altogether. Often framed in tightly enclosed spaces such as doorways, nightclub booths, or peep-show stages, their compressed, claustrophobic settings evoke a palpable sense of unease while also hinting at unconscious or hidden desires. Blending the surrealism of Magritte with the body horror of filmmaker David Cronenberg , Meissner’s work fearlessly explores the complex emotional and psychological consequences for women of being on display, creating a potent cocktail of apprehension, dread, and curiosity. Natalia Gonzalez Martin B. 1995, Madrid. Lives and works in London. Cascara II , 2024 Natalia Gonzalez Martin Richard Saltoun Painted on wood panels using egg tempera and rabbit skin glue, the exquisitely detailed paintings of Natalia Gonzalez Martin hark back to medieval icons, Renaissance altarpieces, and illuminated manuscripts. However, the atmosphere she creates within these confined spaces remains compellingly odd, infused with a healthy dose of Magrittean Surrealism, ambiguity, and eroticism. Filtered through the lens of her Catholic upbringing, Gonzalez Martin renders everyday objects strange, poetic, or mystical. She often isolates body parts or objects, placing them in flat, shadowless voids, disrupting the viewer’s sense of reality. And, while her paintings sometimes hint at religious ritual and symbolism, their meaning is much more opaque, evoking both past and present, divine and secular, suggesting that there are other ways to exist within the world. Zhou Song B. 1982, Jiangxi, China. Lives and works in Beijing. Wisdom Tree I, 2025 Zhou Song Maddox Gallery Holy Light, 2024 Zhou Song Volery Gallery A mind-bending mixture of hyperrealism and surreal flights of fancy, Zhou Song’s remarkable oil paintings explore both the anxieties and the sense of possibility engendered by an age of constant technological acceleration. In his work, natural and artificial elements are distorted and reconfigured in uncanny new forms as the world we know unravels before our eyes. In Wisdom Tree I (2025), for instance, pencils coil through trees like branches, while in other works, candles twist together like snakes, and a rabbit balances a tower of hats on its back. His “New Nature” series (2020–26) is like Magritte reimagined for the post-human age, and borrows freely from the Belgian artist’s iconic repertoire of motifs. Men in suits, apples, bowler hats, and blue skies full of clouds all feature prominently. Indeed, Homeland (2020) is a direct homage to Magritte’s famous painting The Great War (1964). Kristen Sanders B. 1989, California. Lives and works in St. Paul, Minnesota. Shell/Tool, 2023 Kristen Sanders Asya Geisberg Gallery Hand and Flint, 2023 Kristen Sanders Moosey Magritte’s work often explored the gulf between the physical body and the consciousness within it, and the vividly colored paintings of Kristen Sanders operate in a similar psychological space, reframing it for an era in which artificial intelligence is quickly becoming a reality. The world she conjures is one of mystery and uncertainty—a kind of fever dream in which past and future, human and mechanical, have merged, and the viewer is never sure exactly what they are seeing. A sense of Magrittean surrealism pervades her work. In Stone/Shift (2023), the face of a humanoid robot is obscured by a piece of sheer silk, while in Body Thing (2023) a hand holds a fragment of a human face, its single eye staring helplessly out at the viewer. And A Sense of Reality (2023), in which a piece of flint hovers in mid air against a cloudy sky, makes a direct reference to Magritte’s The Castle of the Pyrenees (1959).

title: Louis Vuitton launches Keith Haring handbag collection.
summary: Louis Vuitton has unveiled the eighth chapter of its Artycapucines collection, dedicating 13 new bag designs to the work of Keith Haring . Developed in collaboration with the Keith Haring Foundation, the collection features the late artist’s vibrant visual language—including his signature “Running Heart,” “ Radiant Baby ,” dancing figures, and exuberant graphic compositions. These motifs are translated into designs using different craft techniques, from traditional leather marquetry to cutting-edge laser printing. Haring, who was born in Pennsylvania in 1958 and died in 1990, became one of the defining voices of New York’s downtown art scene in the 1980s, creating graphic works that moved fluidly between street art , gallery walls, and broader culture. His work, characterized by bold outlines, rhythmic figures, and a sense of collective joy, is some of the most recognizable in post-war American art. Beyond the art world, Haring’s imagery has retained a broad cultural presence. His figures have appeared on everything from UNIQLO T-shirts to stadium murals, and his work continues to be cited by a generation of artists, designers, and musicians. The new designs continue the collaboration between the Keith Haring Foundation and the French fashion house. Earlier this year, Louis Vuitton presented clothing printed with Haring’s designs at its womenswear presentation at New York’s Frick Collection . Highlights of the new 13-piece collection include the Capucines Nano Running Heart, a minaudière , or vanity case , crafted in silver-tone metal and set with more than 12,000 hand-placed rhinestones; and the Capucines MM Genesis, inspired by a Louis Vuitton suitcase hand-customised by Haring in 1984. The Capucines East-West Mini Maze, is brought to life through intricate bead embroidery, and the Capucines BB Figures feature Haring’s dancing figures on pristine white Taurillon leather, his characteristic black outline integrated into the bag’s architecture. Louis Vuitton’s Artycapucines Collection, which launched in 2019, now comprises more than 50 designs by artists including Takashi Murakami , Tschabalala Self , Urs Fischer , and Park Seo-Bo . All 13 pieces from the Haring edition will be released as limited editions in Louis Vuitton stores worldwide from January 1, 2027.

title: An Art Lover’s Guide to Paris
summary: Paris has always drawn the art-loving crowd, seduced by the city’s layered history, abundance of museums, and famous beauty. For much of the 20th century, it sat at the center of the art world, helping shape movements including Fauvism , Cubism , and Surrealism . The French capital is often likened to a living museum, but it is also very much a contemporary city, and, in recent years, has reasserted itself as a force in the international art market. Galleries and dealers have expanded or arrived in the city, while a new generation of private museums and foundations has reshaped its institutional landscape, from the Fondation Louis Vuitton and the Pinault Collection at the Bourse de Commerce to the Fondation Cartier ’s new home opposite the Louvre. The shift also owes much to the arrival of Art Basel Paris , which launched in October 2022, originally as Paris+ par Art Basel, replacing the long-standing fair FIAC and cementing Paris as an art world destination each fall. Today, the city’s appeal lies precisely in the collision: Centuries of art history coexist with one of Europe’s most energetic contemporary gallery scenes. In fact, a 2023 study found that 70 percent of recently exhibited artists in France are emerging or mid-career: The city is charging into a new era while remaining, unmistakably, itself. Paris cannot be captured in one guide. What follows is an art lover’s shortcut: the neighborhoods, institutions, and haunts to know first, and where to head from there. The key neighborhoods for art lovers in Paris Four broad areas anchor Paris’s gallery scene, from the extraordinary density of the Marais to the industrial spaces pushing beyond the city’s northeastern edge. The Marais Spread across the 3rd and 4th arrondissements, the Marais is the center of Paris’s contemporary scene. It is the kind of neighborhood where an afternoon can disappear behind a succession of anonymous doors, cobbled courtyards, and former hôtels particuliers . If there’s a buzzer, don’t be shy about ringing it. It’s anchored by a cluster of midsize and heavyweight galleries in the Haut Marais and around rue du Turenne, including Emmanuel Perrotin ’s flagship, which opened here in 2005. Nearby are Almine Rech and MASSIMODECARLO ’s Pièce Unique, which has a compact format devoted to focused presentations. From there, walk toward Place des Vosges for Mendes Wood DM , or north toward Thaddaeus Ropac . The concentration only intensifies around rue du Temple and rue Vieille du Temple, where Galerie Max Hetzler , Marian Goodman Gallery , GALLERIA CONTINUA , and David Zwirner have spaces. Continue north through the Haut Marais for MAĀT Gallery , Templon , Galerie Christophe Gaillard , Suzanne Tarasieve , Galerie Les filles du calvaire , Galerie Marguo , AFIKARIS , and 193 Gallery . Semiose , closer to the Pompidou, is another worthwhile stop, while the historic Jeanne Bucher Jaeger maintains a space on rue de Saintonge. The range is part of the appeal. Blue-chip galleries sit a few minutes from younger programs with distinct curatorial identities, so the Marais offers perhaps the easiest snapshot of the contemporary market in a single afternoon. Institutionally, it is anchored by the Musée Picasso and Centre Pompidou . The latter’s famous Beaubourg building closed completely in September 2025 for renovation and is scheduled to reopen in 2030, with its programming dispersed through its “constellation” of partner venues in the meantime. Matignon, the Golden Triangle, and Place Vendôme Just north of the Champs-Élysées and west of the Palais de l’Élysée, avenue Matignon has transformed into a compact corridor of international galleries. Mennour , White Cube , Almine Rech , Galerie Lelong , Perrotin , and Tornabuoni Art all operate here or immediately nearby, while Hauser & Wirth occupies a 19th-century building on rue François 1er and Gagosian has a gallery on rue de Ponthieu. GALLERIA CONTINUA has also added a Faubourg Saint-Honoré location. Extend the walk east toward Place Vendôme and the Tuileries, where Esther Schipper occupies a discreet courtyard space, and Gagosian has a gallery on rue de Castiglione. The feel is decidedly more polished than the Marais—less wandering, more appointment booking—but the density of heavyweight programs makes it rewarding. Pair a gallery morning with the Grand Palais , Petit Palais , Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris , or Palais de Tokyo . Saint-Germain-des-Prés Over on the Left Bank, Saint-Germain is still inseparable from its post-war literary mythology, café culture, and long history of dealing in modern art, antiques, and design. But its gallery ecosystem is more varied than its old-school reputation suggests. Mennour operates several spaces around rue Saint-André-des-Arts and rue du Pont de Lodi, while rue de Seine remains a spine for galleries including Galerie Georges-Philippe & Nathalie Vallois and Galerie Dina Vierny . The latter opened on rue Jacob in 1947 and remains one of the neighborhood’s defining addresses. Loeve&Co , on rue des Beaux-Arts, specializes in reassessing overlooked figures and episodes of 20th-century art, while Ketabi Bourdet , tucked into passage Dauphine, moves fluently between art, collectible design, architecture, and scenography. This cross-pollination is the point. Saint-Germain is less about a succession of conventional white cubes than conversations between fine art, design, furniture, books, and objects. The neighborhood also maintains close ties to the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts , whose alumni include Matisse , Degas , and Seurat . The east and northeast: the 11th, Belleville, Pantin, and Aubervilliers Paris’s contemporary geography keeps pushing outward. Around the 11th arrondissement, Danysz Gallery , MAGNIN-A , and Galerie Patrick Seguin reward a detour: Their programs range from emerging and urban practices to modern architecture and design. Further east, lower rents and larger industrial spaces created room for galleries such as Crèvecœur and 22,48m² in Belleville. Beyond the périphérique, Thaddaeus Ropac operates a vast Pantin space suited to exhibitions impossible to stage in the Marais, while POUSH in Aubervilliers and Fondation Fiminco in Romainville have helped turn the northeastern edge of Greater Paris into fertile territory for studios, residencies, and ambitious installations. Ropac’s Pantin gallery alone makes the trip worthwhile when the exhibition is right. There is also Gagosian at Le Bourget, an appointment-only, industrial-scale outpost near the airport. Taken together, these spaces make a useful corrective to the postcard version of Paris: Some of the city’s most interesting art experiences now happen well beyond its historic center. The museums and institutions to know in Paris Musée du Louvre : Perhaps the world’s most famous museum, the Louvre houses a vast collection of paintings, sculptures, drawings, and objects across nine curatorial departments, including Islamic Art, Near Eastern Antiquities, and Byzantine and Eastern Christian Art. Musée d’Orsay : Housed in a former Beaux-Arts train station built for the 1900 World’s Fair, the Musée d’Orsay holds the largest and most important collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art ever assembled. Masterpieces by Cézanne , Degas, Van Gogh , Renoir , and Monet are among the highlights. Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris: The city-owned museum’s permanent collection features more than 15,000 paintings, sculptures, installations, and photographs, largely works by the École de Paris ( Modigliani , Chagall , Matisse, Brâncuși ), alongside works up to the present. While the Pompidou is closed (until 2030), the Musée d’Art Moderne will host the Prix Marcel Duchamp . In the opposite wing of its 1937 Art Deco structure is the Palais de Tokyo , a multidisciplinary space with no permanent collection that programs temporary modern and contemporary exhibitions. Fondation Louis Vuitton : Opened in 2014 as part of LVMH’s art and culture arm, the Fondation programs blockbuster exhibitions, site-specific commissions on the Frank Gehry–designed façade, live performances, and events. A nonprofit space with a mission to bring modern and contemporary art to a larger audience. Bourse de Commerce: This former grain and commerce exchange—a cylindrical building painstakingly transformed by Tadao Ando over the course of a decade—is home to the flagship museum of the Pinault Collection, opened in 2021. The private collection of François Pinault, president of Kering, comprises some 10,000 works from the mid–20th century to today, with pieces by Cindy Sherman , Mark Rothko , Jeff Koons , and Urs Fischer alongside a rotating program of exhibitions. Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain: In its new Jean Nouvel –designed home near the Palais Royal, the Fondation Cartier was established in 1984 by the luxury jewelry house and marks France’s first foray into corporate arts patronage. Its collection is heralded for an eclectic approach that combines collecting with commissioning across disciplines. Grand Palais and Petit Palais: This pair of magnificent, glass-domed Beaux-Arts exhibition halls by the Pont Alexandre III were built in 1900 for the World’s Fair. The larger of the two, Le Grand Palais, hosts fairs including Art Basel Paris, Art Paris , and Paris Photo under its famous glass nave throughout the year, alongside temporary exhibitions (often organized in collaboration with neighboring institutions). The Petit Palais is home to the Musée des Beaux-Arts de la Ville de Paris , which houses a collection that spans painting, sculpture, furniture, and objects from ancient times through 1914, including works by Fragonard , Delacroix , and Rembrandt . And beyond: Paris is home to some 130 museums, foundations, and exhibition spaces. Alongside the majors, celebrated institutions worth planning around include the Musée Rodin , L’Orangerie , and the Jeu de Paume ; smaller specialist collections include the Musée de la Vie Romantique , Musée de Montmartre , Musée Bourdelle , and Musée Zadkine . Other foundations and artist museums to know: KADIST , Lafayette Anticipations , and the Giacometti Institute . Where the art world in Paris eats, drinks, and shops For drinks The art of the apéro is sacred in France, and not to be taken lightly. Reliable watering holes for the post-vernissage crowd in the Marais include Le Progrès , Le Mary Celeste , and L’Étincelle . The center of the action is La Perle , a see-and-be-seen spot with an overflowing terrace that turns into a nightly party frequented by the fashion set, the cinema crowd, and vague creative-director types who sip spritzes in clouds of cigarette smoke. Tucked in the corner of Place des Vosges, the Vincent Darré –designed Serpent à Plume is a sexy hideaway for inventive cocktails and late-night revelry, while wine bars elsewhere, like Les Œillets and Vérjus , are more low-key. On the other side of town, expect to spot blue-chip dealers and collectors at Le Fumoir and Le Matignon , or on the terrace of Le Grand Palais’s recently opened Le Grand Café , designed by Joseph Dirand . For dinner Paris’s restaurant landscape has undergone something of a renaissance in recent years, with a shift toward chef-led menus and unexpected ingredients balancing out classic mainstays. Le Servan , Le Dauphin , Soces , and À La Renaissance are illuminating Belleville and the neighboring 11th arrondissement—home to some of the city’s most exciting restaurants right now. After a long day of museum-hopping, head to Café Varenne or Chez Georges for classic French staples done exceptionally well without fanfare, or Pluto inside Lafayette Anticipations, which features a small-plates menu written according to what’s fresh at the market. Quintessential addresses including Le Voltaire and L’Ami Jean often play host to gallery dinners looking to woo collectors, while the veritable Moroccan institution Chez Omar remains a staple for the post-vernissage celebration. For browsing Paris is a literary town, and the city has no shortage of bookshops stocked with monographs, exhibition catalogues, and art books, including Yvon Lambert , 0fr. , and Librairie 7L (established by Karl Lagerfeld ). A wealth of new vintage shops have sprouted along rue de Turenne offering Y2K-revival fashion, but none are doing it like Noir Kennedy or Thanx God I’m a VIP , which has a name and signage that feel intentional in their homage to John Giorno. While the mythical boutique Colette is no more, Scandinavian concept store The Broken Arm —which borrows its name from the Marcel Duchamp readymade—has taken up the torch as one of the city’s most beloved shopping destinations, alongside Centre Commercial . For one-of-a-kind finds, Dary’s , just off Place Vendôme, is exceptional for high jewelry, while Brigitte Tanaka ’s playful organza bags are covetable and unexpected. Where to stay For those who can’t get enough art, Hôtel Amour and The Drawing Hotel give artists carte blanche to use their rooms and hallways as blank canvases—bespoke sleeping quarters sure to spark creative dreams. For an equally inspiring but more minimalist stay, check in to Château Voltaire , Hôtel Massé , Hôtel Hana , or book one of the five suites at the Hôtel Particulier Montmartre for something more discreet. Top tips for art lovers visiting Paris When to go: Paris is at its best in every season, though the shoulder months of April, May, September, and October are ideal: fewer crowds, and alignment with major exhibition openings. Art Basel Paris in October is the anchor moment for the international art crowd. How to navigate: The metro is fast and efficient, but nothing beats the bicycle. Hop on one of the city’s many bike shares and make use of the protected bike lanes that have sprouted across Paris in recent years. Those on foot should be mindful of not blocking these pathways. What locals know: Most museums, foundations, and institutions close weekly on Monday or Tuesday. Plan accordingly, and reserve tickets in advance to avoid the crowds. A Paris Museum Pass grants access to most major institutions and heritage sites. Gallery hours are sometimes just suggestions, so email ahead for smaller spaces. Openings aren’t restricted to Thursday nights: Many happen across the stretch from Wednesday to Saturday. And Paris rewards slow travel. Leave time to get lost and follow your eye. Bringing work home: Exporting contemporary art from France is generally straightforward. The country’s blue-chip galleries handle international shipping routinely, and English is widely spoken in commercial galleries. Note that works over 50 years old with certain valuations may require an export license ( certificat pour un bien culturel or licence d’exportation ), which galleries can help facilitate. VAT rules apply differently for EU vs. non-EU buyers; ask the gallery to walk you through.

title: Ed Ruscha designs poster for Alejandro González Iñárritu’s “Digger,” starring Tom Cruise.
summary: Ed Ruscha has designed the poster for Alejandro González Iñárritu’s new dark comedy film Digger (2026) starring Tom Cruise, which opens in theaters Friday, Oct. 2nd, in the U.S. and U.K. The artist unveiled the design Sunday at an event at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), attended by Cruise, Iñárritu, and cast members including John Goodman, Jesse Plemons, Michael Stuhlbarg, and Ross Hatt. The poster sets the film’s title vertically at center, rendered in Ruscha‘s own typeface , against a slate-gray backdrop dominated by a looming iceberg. Phrases including “A Man. A Plan. A Meltdown.” and “Comedy equals tragedy plus time” are arranged around the central image. Digger follows an oil tycoon whose Greenland drilling rig triggers an explosion that dislodges an ice shelf, setting off a global disaster. Ruscha called the film “kaleidoscopic in its message and its content and its humor” after seeing it at a screening roughly six months ago. “I knew I had seen an epic production, an epic product from an epic producer,” he said. “So I jumped at the idea of doing the poster.” At the unveiling, Ruscha joked, “Well, the movie blew my hair back. And not only that, it parted it down the middle. It has since grown back,” according to the Los Angeles Times . Iñárritu, who has admired Ruscha’s work and attended his 2024 LACMA retrospective, said in a statement that the artist “has this rare ability to create an enormous sense of space with very little, to be funny and profound, precise and mysterious, all at once.” In a phone interview with the Times , the director elaborated on the poster's central image, saying, “We think that we are different from nature. So nature, in a way, becomes our enemy. We are fighting a fight against nature, and the enemy is an ice shelf going to Europe.” Cruise also said he had grown up admiring the artist’s work. In 2002, Iñárritu visited Ruscha's Venice studio hoping to cast him in 21 Grams , a plan that ultimately fell through on scheduling. Both have since been honored at LACMA’s annual Art+Film Gala, Ruscha in 2012 and Iñárritu in 2015. Iñárritu has twice exhibited installation work at the museum, including CARNE y ARENA in 2017 and Sueño Perro earlier this year. Ruscha, represented by Gagosian , has long adapted the language of Hollywood and cinema as subject matter, from his text-based “HOLLYWOOD” drawings to a body of experimental short films of his own. “This is a beautiful encounter of art and film,” LACMA director Michael Govan said at the unveiling.

title: Art Basel Miami Beach announces 272 exhibitors for its 2026 edition.
summary: Art Basel Miami Beach has announced 272 exhibitors, from over 40 countries and territories, for its 2026 edition. The fair takes place December 4th through 6th at the Miami Beach Convention Center, with invite-only VIP days on December 2nd and 3rd. This year, the fair will introduce a substantially reconfigured showfloor, presenting a more focused gallery lineup across roughly 12 percent less floor space and organizing the fair around four hospitality plazas rather than five. The main Galleries sector will feature about 10 percent fewer exhibitors, with blue-chip galleries once grouped now distributed throughout the show. “The redesign begins with the galleries: how their artists and programs are presented, and how collectors encounter them,” said Bridget Finn, director of Art Basel Miami Beach, in a statement. “Our exhibitors have reinforced the value of a more focused environment, and the smaller footprint is a deliberate choice in service of that. Each presentation will have room to command attention.” More than 30 galleries are participating in the fair for the first time, most through the project-based sectors Nova, Positions, and Survey. Galleries from Latin America and the Caribbean are represented in depth. Brazil once again forms the show's third-largest national contingent at the fair with galleries including Raquel Arnaud , Simões de Assis , Nara Roesler , and A Gentil Carioca participating. Galleries from Los Angeles and Chicago are also well-represented this year, along with an increased presence of galleries from South Florida. Zero 10, Art Basel's initiative for art of the digital era, returns with “Generation,” its largest presentation yet, bringing together 19 projects from 22 galleries and platforms. Curated by Karen Archey with Eli Scheinman, the exhibition includes work by artists such as Jon Rafman , Refik Anadol , and Sarah Meyohas . Former Christie’s head of Digital Art Nicole Sales Giles has joined Art Basel as Zero 10’s first global head, tasked with shaping the initiative's evolution as a year-round platform. Beyond the convention center, the Turrell Art Foundation and Art Basel, supported by Pace Gallery , will unveil a significant new outdoor body of work by James Turrell , free to the public. In Collins Park, Public Art Fund will present “Between Tides,” a participatory exhibition of artist-designed ping-pong tables. The Art Basel Awards also return in partnership with BOSS, with the Gold Awardees to be revealed at the Art Basel Awards Night on Thursday, December 3rd.

title: Rare $3 million David Hockney painting of his dog heading to auction at Christie’s London.
summary: A rare painting by David Hockney of his beloved dachshund Stanley is heading to auction at Christie’s, where it carries a high estimate of £2.5 million ($3.3 million). The work, Dog Painting 17 (1995), shows Stanley curled up asleep on a cushion and is one of more than 40 paintings Hockney made in 1994 and 1995 for his “Dog Series,” devoted entirely to his two dachshunds. It is the first painting from the series ever to come to auction. “This is such an exciting painting for us,” said Tessa Lord, Christie’s head of postwar and contemporary art. “The rarity is kind of extraordinary.” Christie’s believes only six paintings from the series are in private hands, with the rest held by the David Hockney Foundation. The consignor acquired the work after it appeared in a “Dog Series” exhibition at the L.A. Louver gallery in Venice, California, a show that reportedly drew 7,000 visitors in four days. According to Hockney, many brought their own dogs along. Stanley, named after silent film star Stan Laurel, was chosen as a puppy by Hockney in 1987 and rarely left his side. He later adopted a second dachshund named Boodgie. The dogs became fixtures of Hockney’s famously social Hollywood Hills home, where, according to his authorized biographer Christopher Simon Sykes, the artist was untroubled by their lack of house training. One friend, Jonathon Brown, recalled the dogs relieving themselves in Hockney's shoes, and, on one occasion, on the floor of actor Dennis Hopper ’s Frank Gehry–designed house in Venice. Hockney's response, as Brown told it, was characteristically unbothered, “Oh, it'll be dry in the morning, luv, and you can just pick it up.” Hopper, Brown said, “chose silence, but he looked like murder.” Hockney began painting Stanley and Boodgie at a difficult moment, after losing several friends to AIDS-related illness and, in particular, following the death of his close friend, the curator Henry Geldzahler, from pancreatic cancer. Hockney later said he had wanted “desperately to paint something loving.” Lord described the “Dog” Series” in similar terms, saying “He felt such a loss of love; this was kind of a catharsis for him.” Of Dog Painting 17 specifically, she pointed to its “incredible spontaneity” and “fluidity of brushstrokes,” noting the texture built up beneath the cushion and “that slight flick of the ear that really animates Stanley.” She added: “I love the fact that there is this kind of innocence to it, but it is so much more than that. There’s a universality to it… It's so much more than just a portrait of a dog.” Hockney was hardly alone among artists in finding inspiration in a pet dachshund—both Andy Warhol and Pablo Picasso doted on the breed. Picasso's dachshund Lump appears in his studies for his painting Las Meninas (1957), and Warhol was frequently photographed with his own. ” “Dog Painting 17” carries an estimate of £1.5 million to £2.5 million ($1.99 million to $3.3 million) and will be sold on October 14, during Frieze Week in London, following the artist’s death this past June at 88. The painting will go on public view, free of charge, at Christie's London galleries beginning October 8th.

title: What Sold at The Armory Show 2026
summary: The Armory Show wrapped up its 2026 edition on Sunday, September 27th, following four days at the Javits Center that brought some 50,000 visitors to the fair. This year’s edition arrived later than usual on New York’s art world calendar, shifting from its traditional early September slot to the end of the month, and expanded to 242 exhibitors from more than 30 countries. Under director Kyla McMillan, the fair also grew its Presents and Solo sections, devoted to emerging galleries and single-artist presentations, respectively. There were several other firsts. The fair debuted Armory After Hours (a carnival-inspired procession through the aisles led by a DJ and live percussionists), and staged its largest prize program to date. That included new acquisition initiatives with Pérez Art Museum Miami and the Bronx Museum , the latter of which acquired Zoë Pulley ’s Elegance No. 1 (2026) for $14,000 from Superposition Gallery , one of Artsy’s best booths from the fair . Elegance No. 1, 2026 Zoë Pulley Superposition Spring (81), 2026 Zoë Pulley Superposition This year’s edition featured sales across a particularly wide range of price points. The most expensive disclosed transaction was a Jackson Pollock painting sold by Hollis Taggart for between $3 million and $3.5 million, while several galleries reported seven-figure sales by artists including Joan Mitchell , Tracey Emin , and Jean-Michel Basquiat . The fair also placed an emphasis on the Caribbean and its diaspora, with booths and large-scale installations addressing migration, memory, and regional identity, including presentations by artists such as Gio Swaby , Kachelle Knowles , Lizania Cruz , Joshua Nazario , and Bony Ramirez . “The energy at The Armory Show this year was palpable,” McMillan told Artsy. “Collectors, dealers, curators, and visitors alike returned with optimism and excitement for the fall art season.
